The Area described in the Schedule to this Order is hereby declared to be an area infected with swine- fever for the purnoses of the Swine-Fever (Infected Areas) Order of 1896. 2. This Order shall come into operation on the Ninth day of January. one thousand nine hundred and one. In witness whereof the Board of Agriculture have hereunto set their Official Seal this Second day of January, one thousand nine hundred and one.

The fichu is more than 100 years old, and probably it has never, throughout its long exist- ence, been as various as it is now. It may some- times be worn bertha-fashion; some are high in the neck at the back, but so much open in front that the waist is reached before the two sides meet. A variety has long ruffled ends, which fall to the hem of the gown; and an evening dress for a girl of 14 or 15, is in pale blue Canton silk with wide insertions of lace on both skirt and bodice. Horizontal on the former, they serve as a sort of heading to the accordeon-pleated flounce, made of the same material as the dress.

hats and toques seem to demand an ornament, as a counterpoise on the shoulders for theirtop-heavy appearance. A ruffle looks prettiest iaoream or oyster coloured taffetas, bordered with hatf-inch wide sable, and long strands or ropesof coarse net in front, caught in here and there with sable hencle and tails. The mingling of f3panish lace, with its shimmering silken sheen—l speak of the cream lace—is an effective mixture with sable or mink. We have been somewhat in- clined to shelve this handsome fabric in favour of thread laces; but anyone who is lucky enough to possess Spanish or blonde laces would do well to contemplate their virtues. and then it is asserted that blue serge is going out of fashion; but the truth is that it is as much worn as ever in the morning and afternoon by-country ladies, as well as by a good proportion of those in town. A well-cut, tailor-made serge suit is as indispensable to the wardrobe of the well-dressed woman as a black silk was some twenty years ago. Nor does it seem likely that dark blue serge will become unfashionabe for many a year, though tweed and cloth and frieze have et come to the front of late. A good navy serge dresahas,a red cloth waistcoat and collar, with a few rows 'of narrow black velvet run upon both, and also on the red cloth cuffs turned up from the wrists upon the sleeves. Another blue serge, with wile diagonal rib, and a very soft texture, has a bolero-with long ends pointed and falling over a folded band of blue and green panne. The vest is white cloth, with a small chessboard pattern in blade and palest blue. For the evening wear of matrons crepo-de-Chine is very popular. It is of such exquisite texture, especially ill the more expensive qualities, that it drapes better than any other fabric in which a similar quantity of silk is interwoven. I saw a pale pink crepe-de-Chine, the skirt of which is gathered upon the hips in close lines. The fulness that results from this falls on either side a lace panel in the centre of the skirt, and a number of narrow frills throw it out from the feet in the fashionable manner. The pink of the crepe and the ivory tone of the lace contrast very pleasantly. Narrow black velvet in a series of bows is carried round the top of the frills.

div.p: [FARRIS'S, 28-30, BERRY STREET, LIVERPOOL.
"STRUCK ILE 'LAT KLONDYKE. A Lucky St. Helens Man.

Edwar,l Wallace, a young fallow, aged twenty-eight years, has jos) returned to this country from Klondyke forthe winter. He quaintly says that he has made enough to " keep him tor the rest of his life " during the two years he has been out there, but when a man gets a few dollars' he wants double the number,and so on,and next spring he will return to Dawson City to again try his luck. His fath t was a travelling acrobat, and Edward was born in Liverpool at the old Lime-street Station Hotel, which has long since disappeared. His boyhood and youth were spent in St. Helens, but when he attained his majority he emigrated to America. When the rush to Mondyke took place in 1897 his brother went out there and struck " lie." Edward joined him early In 1899, and they for some time worked together. Edward experienced the same difficulties as others in getting to Dawson City, but instead of essaying the long trail, in attempting we') Zr'lny a poor fellow has lost his life, he did the distance with a dog team, carrying with him a tent, waterproof, and fir branches for his night shelter. A few months in Dawson City, and Edward " felt, his feet." and trird his own luck in " Walch's " Creek, in British Columbia, where there is a rich and lucrative alluvial deposit. In that "claim "he averaged about a dozen ounces of gold per diem, his greatest output on One day while there being forty ounces. He then shifted 500 miles north, to a place called Hillside, on the Bonanza. Here his find- ings were much better, including numerous five-ounce or six-ounce nuggets. During his diggings he came across many fossils, and a mammoth's tusk, forty feet long. He worked away until last September, and then began his journey to this country., covering by the de- toar be took 16,000 miles. He confirms the reports as to the severity of the winter weather in KlOndyke— often 60 degrees below zero. Thteseummeter between is pleasant, with a temeraur 170 and 80 degrees, but he says the mosqui- toes are a perfect plague. He says the climate is splendid, and that you can walk thirty miles with less fatigue than you can cwer twelve miles in this country. Living is very expensive there— a dollar and a half for a meal and a dollar for a bed. He and his brother bonght ins store of provisions in the summer time, which carried them over the winter, and thus saved a lot of money. It was impossible to work much in the winter. Men who do anything by band have to content thamselveS with accumulating deposit in the winter months—October till March—and washing it when the sun thaws it in the summer. Even with machinery only a little can be done in the winter time. He says it is folly for a 'nor man to go out there in the hope of making a fortune, but people with money have a crand chaoce of amassing wealth if they are pre- pared to rough it.

RUBY LOVEDAY
B T SILAS K. HOCKING, Author of "The Strange Adventures of Israel rendray," "The Day of Recompense," "God's Outcast," In Spite of Fate," "Her Benny," SE.o.

SYNOPSIS OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS : The Lovedays, rich strangers from London, take fur- nished apartments at Endilloe Farm, tenanted by the Pentyres, a half-ruined family. Young Justin Pentyre is discontented at the prospect of their poverty being observed, and endeavours unsuccess- fully to persuade his people to refuse the offer.

div.head: CHAPTER 111. 111:111T.
div.p: CHAPTER 111. 111:111T.
"She's all my fancy painted her; She's lovely, she's divine."

Justin had no occasion to steel his heart, how- ever, for Ruby was not of the party. She was too tired for a walk, after her long railway journey, and preferred to remain in the house and finish a. book she was reading. Mr. Loveday caught sight of Dorothy directly he emerged from the plantation; and came at once towards her, followed by Mrs. Lovediy and Nathan Ilendy, Mr. Pentyre's hind and man-of-all-work. Nathan was only too pleased to assume the position of guide, philosopher, and friend to the new arrivals from London, and to shew them all the beauties of Endilloe and surrounding neigh- bourhood. Nathan was something of an oracle in his way, and like most such oracles, believed that people who were born and brought up in cities were in a state of the most lamentable and pitiable ignorance. This thesis Nathan had proved again and again—to his own satisfaction, at any rate, if not to the satisfaction of other people, and was prepared to prove it again on the shortest possible notice.

"Take pigs," Nathan would say, "by way of example Now, what do town's people know 'bout pigs? As a fact, they don't knew nothin'. Why, a chap from some big town up the country, wance axed me ef we sheared 'em for wool. Then take the weather. Their hignorance on that subject es terrible—an' the wust is they keep puttin' of it in the papers. But there! what can ee expect from people brought up in sich places!" In this way Nathan would defend his proposition against all comers, and in his heart thanked Heaven that he had been born in the country and not in any of those benighted towns. The advent of his master's paying guests, Nathan hailed with great pleasure, and. was delighted that on the very first evening he had the opportunity of shewing them round the neighbourhood. It was- a little disappointment -to Nathan that they asked to be taken straight to the sea. He had • so many other things to shew them of far greater interest. There were pigs, and poultry, and sheep, and a prize heifer, to say nothing of various crops in the fields. But, no. The tall, handsome gentleman, in his light check suit and cloth cap, had no wish to be taken into- the yard or the fields. He wanted to get on the cliffs at the nearest point, where he could smell the salt air and enjoy the sight of the sea, and his wife was as eager for the sea as him- self.

"Jist like those town's folk," was Nathan's un- spoken comment. "They're jist like ducks—they make for the water fust thing; but then, what can 'ee expect of people brought up in sich places!" So Nathan, in a very demure, not to say sorrow- ful, frame of mind, led the way up the slope and through the plantation, until they came out upon the cliffs. Then, to make matters worse, Mr. Loveday appeared to forget his presence. Dorothy at once claimed his attention, then Justin was _ . _ . _ .
introduced, and in a few minute's the four of them

were standing in a row looking off upon the darken- ing stretch of ocean, and talking as freely as though they had known each other all their lives. Nathan stood solitary and ' alone, fifty yards away. Then reflecting that .he was not -wanted, turned slowly and retraced his steps to Endilloe. Justin, notwithstanding all his protestations to Dorothy, was considerably disappointed that the young lady had not coins out with her parents, Whether Dorothy had intended it or nof she had succeeded in rousing his curiosity. A pret+y maiden is always an interesting object to a young man, and after all that Dorothy had said, he wotdd have been less than human had he not felt more or
less c:i-rious to see such a dainty and bewitching

creature. Us soon forgot his disappointment, however. Mr. and Mrs. Loveday proved to be such agreeable company that he was sorry when the slowly gather- ing darkness compelled them to return. It is true they talked about nothing in particular. But the charm of conversation is not so much in the matter as in the manner. Mr. Evan Loveday was a capable, well-read, up-to-date City man, and he pretended to be nothing more nor less. That he had been successful—after the manner of what the world calls success—there could be no doubt; but purse-proud he was not. Justin found all his prognostications falsified during the first five minutes. The City merchant and the country salesman met on equal ground. The question of social difference did not occur to either of them, least of all to Evan Loveday; and when they parted at the orchard gate, Justin found all his prejudices scattered to the winds. "Well," questioned Dorothy, when the Lovedays were out of hearing, "what is your verdict ? "
"I must confess they are very agreeable people," he answered. -

"I thought you would say so. But what a pro- vidence for you that Ruby did not come out." "Why so ? " "Because you would have lost your heart by this time," and she ran laughing into the house. In the big roomy kitchen which had now to answer the double purpose of dining-room and drawing-room, Mrs. Pentyre and her husband were discussing with great animation the, advent of the strangers, or more particularly the advent of Ruby. For as yet John Pentyre had not seen Mr. and Mrs. Loveday. Ruby, it would appear, having finished her book, and getting tired of being alone, had come off into the kitchen in search of company. Mrs. Pentyre nearly dropped, as she expressed it, when the door silently opened, and the dainty apparition, most bewitchingly attired, advanced into the room. John rose from his seat in the big chimney-nook, and took his pipe slowly from between his teeth, much wondering what was the proper thing for him to do or say under the circumstances. Not being able to answer that question satisfactorily, he stood stock- still, and said nothing. "Why, my dear," said Mrs. Pentyre, in her motherly way, lifting up her hands deprecatingly, "a kitchen with a stone floor is not the proper place for such as you "Oh, I don't mind the stone floor in the least," was the smiling answer; "but what a dear, glorious old room. You won't mind my coming in will you ? " "Oh, dear, no; come, and welcome. John, get a chair for the young lady." "No, please, Mr. Pentyre, don't trouble. I'm quite rested now. Father and mother, you know, have gone MT in search of the sea." "Yes, I know. I sent Nathan to shew them the way." "Is it far ? " she questioned, looking up at him with a smile. "Oh, no, just over the top of the hill beyond the plantation; but the easiest way to get on the beach, is to go down the valley, which twists round into Poldula Porth." _

"I felt too tired to go myself," she ' answered, after a Dause ; "besides, I wanted to finish my book, and then I shall have plenty of time to see everything, shan't I ?" "Oh, yes, I hope sp," he answered, slowly, still holding his pipe between his finger and thumb, and wondering if it would be considered rude to finish it in her presence. She was only a girl—and a mere slip of a girl at that, as he admitted to him- self afterwards. Yet, somehow, he felt consider- ably overawed in her presence. "Oh, yes, you will have plenty of time," he went on, uneasily, "for, after all, there isn't much to be seen in a place like this. I'm afraid you'll find it terrible

--40 h, I don't think so at all, not if the weather keeps fine. But won't you finish your pipe? I'm sure you are letting it go out." "Then you won't mind my smoking?" he said, brightly, and smiling at her. "Oh, dear, no. Father smokes like a Thames ferry-boat, and that's saying a great:deal, isn't it?" "Well, very likely it is, miss," he said, doubt- fully, "very likely it is ; but having never seen it Thames ferry-boat—" "Now, John, you needn't ihe-v, off your ignor- since before the young lady," Mrs. Pentyre inter- rupted, somewhat reproachfully. "But it's this w^.7 Was" she continued, turninit towards Rubs
"I've been trying ror years to get him to take me to London • but he keeps putting it off. I expect some day I shall go without him." _ _ _

"You'd soon want to get back again, I faney," Ruby said, with a smile. "London is a frightfully dull place. We once spent a whole summer in London: Father could not get away, for some reason. Well, believe me, it was worse than the heart of Africa. Everybody goes away in August, you see— But your pipe is out, Mr. Pentyre; allow me. I nearly always light father's cigars when I have the chance. There now—" Mrs. Pentyre hold up her hands in consternation. To think a young lady from London should strike a match and hold it over the bowl of her husband'a pipe until it was alight, while he quietly submitted as though he enjoyed being waited upon! It was •uutrageous She felt too astonished to speak. "My! But you have pretty little hands, miss!" stid, eyeing her taper fingers admiringly. "I reckon you never did very much hard work." Then lie caught his wife's eye and blushed uncomfort- ' ably. "John!" That was all she said, but there was no mistaking the tone, and it spoke volumes to him. For several minutes after that John smoked in silence, while Ruby explored the great kitchen, under the guidance of Mrs. Pentyre, and ultimately disappeared into the dairy to have a look at the butter and cream.

When the door closed behind them and he found himself alone in the great kitchen he fell to thinking. The sight of this fresh, girlish face stirred his heart with old memories. He found himself back again in the days of his youth, living over again those sweet hours of romance that remain among the most priceless of the niemories of life. When Ruby returned his pipe was out again, for he could not smoke and dream at the same time. It was in vain that he protested, in vain that Mrs. Pentyre tried to catch his eye. Ruby per- sisted in re-lighting the pipe, and John admired the white taper fingers a second time, but was careful not to make any remark. But in his heart he said: "Bless her, she's a little beauty." When Dorothy and Justin returned Mrs. Pentyre had got beyond the rebuke stage, and John felt himself at liberty to enlarge on the many charms of their fair visitor. "You ought to have been here, Justin," he said to his son, pulling deep whiffs at his pipe; "she's a sight for weak eyes, she is indeed.' "So she's captured you also, has she ? " he said, indifferently. "I really think I'd better keep out of the way." "That's just what I have been telling you," Dorothy interposed, banteringly. "If you take my advice you will stick to your first resolution." "As far as I know there is no reason why I should not," he answered, "though I am not afraid of any ill effects following my meeting her." "But, joking apart," interposed Mrs. Pentyre, "she is really one of the sweetest little creatures I've ever rteen, and hasn't one bit of pride—" "Not,isti4," interposed John, with emphasis. "Alai fl'ee and friendly as if we were her "You'd hardly think it, but she would insist on lighting my pipe," interrupted John. "And her dress—well, you should have seen it, Dorothy. Of course, it was not fit for a kitchen—" _ _

"But her hands caught my fancy," John remarked from out the chimney nook. "Yes. And, do you know, he told her so," said Mrs. Pentyre, severely, after which conversation became more general. Soon after Justin went off to bed, for he had to be early astir in the morning. But try as he would he could not keep the name of Ruby out of his mind. He had pretended to Dorothy that he did not want to see their fair visitor, and that it was his deliberate intention to keep out of her way. Yet all the time, in spite of himself, he kept drawing imaginary pictures of her, and endowing her with more virtues that even her most intimate friends ever discovered in her. He acknowledged to himself that this was exceedingly silly and quite unworthy- of a man who, up to the age of twenty-two, had kept him. self heart-whole and fancy free. But, silly or not, there was no denying the fact that this unseen and unknown stranger had already begun to exercise an uncomfortable influence upon his mind. Of course, it was all Dorothy's fault. If Dorothy had said nothing about her, and his father and mother had also remained silent he would scarcely have given to her a first thought, much less a second. It was humiliating to be kept awake on the very first night by one whom he had never seen.

Colds and coufthe are the order of the day, and little I woaeer, when We consider the changes to which the British climate subjecte us. When the chest feels sore mina, which have had to be altered in consequence of The arrangements for the wedding of Queen Wilhel- and painful after coughing, a little barley water is very the death of the Grand Duke of Saxe-Weimar, do not soothing. To make this, take one ounce of pearl barley, and bail it in a little water, for a few minutes. Pour off appear to be running altogether smoothly. First it had e f tube postponed to allow of the settlement of conatitu- th water, put in a quart of resh water, and let it tional preliminaries, and this has been followed by the simmer for an hour. It may have a little lemon juice sudden departure of Duke Henry of Mecklenburg from added. " the Hague, owing, it is said, to his having taken offence MADGE." at the manner in which his future position has been dis- cussed in the Dutch Parliament. For all that is said to the contrary Disks Henry is not very popular in Holland. He is not wealthy, and when- ever the expenditure of public money is concerned there are always some legislators who are prepared to say very uncomplimentary things. We know this from ex- perience in our own Parliament,when Royal grants have been discussed, but, unfortunately Duke Henry of Mecklenburg seems to have the misfortune of possessing an unduly sensitive disposition. The bridal attire of Queen Wilhelmina promises to be sumptuoue indeed, The wedding dress Is entirely of cloth of silver, embroidered in a design of orange. blossoms raised in silver threads, with the flowers in seed pearls. This work Was c aried out iei Amsterda J _ the dress is being built in Paris. It is interesting 1 that our own Queen has never, during her long life,gone to Paris for any of her gowns. Very few members ot the Royal Family however, have followed this the Duchess of York alone sharing her qsj:e judicea in this respect. Happily for modern Royal brides,Royal wedding core monies do nct occupy quite so long a time as they did in olden days. To give one example,—when Queen Mary married Philip of Spain, the ceremony in Win- chester Cathedral lasted from eleven o'clock in the morn- ing till three in the afternoon. The Queen was dressed for the occasion in a robe richly brocaded on a gold ground,with a long train bordered with pearls and dia- monds of great brilliancy. The large sleeves were caught up with clusters of gold set with pearls and diamonds, her coif being borderedwith two rows of large diamonds , The kirtle worn beneath the robe was of white satin wrought with silver. Four English lords, in the name of the whole realm, gave away the august bride. A most brilliant weddirg was that of Miss Cassel, and Mr. Wilfrid Ashley, which was celebrated quite recently at St. George's, Hanover Square, the Prince of Wales, and everyone who is anyone in Society circles, being present. It was remarkable for taking place on a Fri- day, thus setting at defiance the old superstition as to the ill-luck of a marriage on th it day, and until this occasion there had been no wedding on a Friday at this fashionable and favourite church, for 25 years. The wedding presents received by Mr and Mrs Wilfrid Ashley were on a most magnificent giale, number- ing between four and five hundred, and estimated to represent about £40,000. In the ordinary course of things, Mrs Ashley will be one of the richest hsiresses of the New Century: She is the only daughter of Sir Ernest Cassel, who is one of our millionaire financiers and if his daughter outlives him, she may inherit a' fortune which is estimated at something like ten millions. The Nineteenth Century; or more strictly speaking,the latter part of it, has opened up a new world for women, in all, or nearly all, the active spheres of life. Even ha Germany, which is one of the most backward of the Western nations in this respect, women are coming to the front in the various professions and occupations, formerly monopolized by the opposite sex. The first young woman has recently taken the degree of Doctor of PhileSophy at the University of Breslau, but not with- out a little homely lecture from the Dean, which shows that the advance of woman is not viewed with much favour in that quarter. He hoped that wemen students would continue tobe the exception, and that they would keep to their " primary and noblest calling," which was —the home. Astounding bargains,"" huge sacrifices," " sweeping reductions,' and other startling announcements greet one at every turn when taking one's walks about shoe- land, and drapery establishments are once more the scene of battles and arguments innumerable. It is really nothing short of marvellous how many gentle- women there are who will indeed descend to a veritable battle when a 1 bareain " is in cpfestion—hut tilt fact remain that they both can and will do ete. When a dispute between two would-be purchaser arises, the unfortunate shop-walker is called up to settle it, and it is seercely to be wondered at that the majority of t'aese individuals look anxious and worried just now. Only the other day an incident of the kind described occurred at a large West End drapery hems°. A woman pounced upon a blouse bet another stending close by said she had already secured it. Both fought for pos- session, and ere the shopwalker could reach the scene of action the garment was in two parts. Nzet c tme the knotty point as to which woman was to pay for it. Both declieed, and it ended in their being requested by one of the heads of the establishment, to leave the shop: Both these women were well-dressed, and well-spoken, yet seemed in no way to realise the disgrace of their posi- tion. Such is th • effect a bargain can have on the:ecind feminine.

Fashions in skirts and sleeves will have undergone a consid-rable change ere spring is with us, and we should therefore beware of such purchases. But lengths of silk sufficient far blouses (taking into account tke larger sleeves) or underskirts, are always useful, and the care- ful "bargain hunter," cannot go far wrong lathe matter of gloves, hosiery, lace, and the divers items unaffected by the changing molds of Dame Fashion. F:oral tcques with muffs to match are much in evi- -1 dence. not having waited until spring, to put in their re- appearance. Chryeauthemun- a are perhaps the favourite blooms at the moment for biS particular purpose, but roses run them very sr These flowers take many ' hues, quite unknown to ature, but the fact that none of us ever saw pastel-hi brown, or turquoise roses on a branch, does not prevent such floral freaks looking very comely when resting in a cloud of tulle, or chiffon, on a daintily arranged coiffure. MI up-to-date beads are " dry-:deaned," This is accomplished by a process of steaming under a thin rubber bag, which fits the head tightly, The drying is done with an electric brush, after which the hair is delicately perfumed. The process is delightful, but one nreds to take precautions against catching cold after- wards.

div.head: BIG BLAZE.
div.p: A BIG BLAZE.
Hardware Dealer's Premises Gutted in But: er- market-street.

The premises of Mr. William Beswick, hardware factor, oil dealer, &s, 21, Buttermarket-street, Warring- ton were the scene of a serious fire early on Friday morning. It appears that information of the nuMoreak was received at the Fire Station at 5.30 and having regard to the inflammable nature of the stock on the prernis,a, the full strength of the brigade turned out with the engine t. Captain, reels,and ladders under the direction of Deputy Superbo tendent Turner. The Sup,rintendent was unable to turn out, owing to indisposition. On arriving at the shop it was found that the building, which is three storeys high and the whole of the rear portion of the premises were ablaze. Four or five powerftf. jets were quickly got to work from the mains, lou!: ovirog, to the Smoke, and the congested stare of the building, the firemen had great difficulty in locating the fire. A horse was safely removed from the stable attache] to the shop. The brigade worked extremely hard and the fire was got in hand shortly after 8 .'cluck. A number of men remained on the premises during the greater part of the day, playing on the smouldering debris. Toe conflagration wrought great damage, five rooms and their contents being completely gutted. Sense of Mr. Beswiek's store- rooms are on the second floort of the shops of Miss Nicol, wool dealer, and Mr I,r,ughlin, jeweller, and unfor- tunately the stock in these shops,was damaged by the water dripping from the rooms above. The rdigin of the fire is unknown. Mr Viniliam Besavisk, junior, left the prenniFes late the previous ni,ht, and everything then seemed to be in its usual condition. The amount of the damage is as yet unknown, but it is estimated that it cannot be less than £l,OOO. Fortunately it is fully covered by insurance. div.head: CHAPTER IV. DISAPPOINTMENT.
div.p: CHAPTER IV. DISAPPOINTMENT.

"My curiosity gets the better of me, And steals my sleep.": a During the next week it seemed to Justin as though Miss Loveday deliberately kept out of his way. Try as he would he could not get a glimpse of her. When he left in the morning she was not yet stirring, and when he returned in the evening she was either engrossed with a book or else had gone off on some excursion with her father and did not return until after dark, so that by the end of a week he had not so much as seen the flutter of one of her pretty frocks. This was all the more annoying since the other members of the family saw her constantly, and had something to say every evening relative to her sweetness and good nature. Justin listened to her praises in dogged silence, and pretended not to be in the least interested; though he was, in reality, much more piqued than he would have admitted even to himself. . _

He began to think after awhile that Miss Ruby had either overheard his conversation with Dorothy or else that Dorothy had inadvertently or uncon- sciously betrayed his sentiments, and that the stranger was, in cousequence, standing on her dignity and giving him to understand that she was sublimely indifferent to his existence, and was less anxious to see him than he was to see her. He would have asked Dorothy if he dared if Miss Loveday was aware of his existence. But he could not do that without betraying an interest that he had all along professed he did not feel. If he had talked less beforehand, he need not have been so reticent now. He was being well paid, out for his pride and stupidity. He made one or two earnest attempts to banish the subject from his mind. After all, what did it matter to him? The Lovedays did not belong to his world. From what his cousin, Phil Pasmore, had said, they were rich people, and lived in con- sid‘.rable style somewhere in the West End of Lonein. They had come to Endilloe for a couple of inmAs for change of air and rest—though it was una.-rstood that Mr. Loveday would go up to town ever: now and then on business—and when thetime was up they would go back to London again, and in all probability they would never see them or hear of theit again. Under the circum- stances what did it matter to him if he never saw Miss Loveday? And it was worse than foolishness to waste a, single thought upon her. • But though his reasoning was eminently sound, and no one could cast doubt on the wisdom of hia resolutions, he was not long in discovering, what most people have discovered, that human nature is not to be ruled by logic, and that if reason says you should not go a certain way that is the way of all others you most desire to go. Justin looked at all the front windows every morning, when leaving for Trelford, particularly at the window of the room that Miss Loveday occupied, but the blind was invariably down. Evidently she was not particularly fond of early rising. Thursday was early-closing day at Trel- ford, and as he hurried homeward between two and three in the afternoon he felt quite confident that that day, at any rate, his curiosity would be I rewarded. Dorothy came to meet him, as her I tustom was when she was not busy. "4.3r0u ought to have got home an hour earlier, Snstin," she said, "and then you would have seen the Lovedays drive off in style." "Gone, have they ? " he questioned, with a. I curious sensation of sinking at the heart. "They've driven over to Newquay to visit some I friends of theirs who are staying there."

-'741;;;; did they get a carriage ?" "Had it sent over from Trelford ; and a hand- some turn-out it was. ,Coachman in livery and a splendid pair of horses. I did not think the White Hart could have done it in such good style." k; "Evidently you don't know what Trefford is capable of," he said, with a smile. "But the carriage was nothing to Miss Loveday. You should have seen her, Justin."
"Indeed ! " "She was a perfect picture. Really, Justin, she is the loveliest creature you ever saw." "But I have not seen her," he said, with pre- tended indifference.

"That is the reason you ought to have been at home an hour earlier. She was dressed all in white—white lace dress, white boots, white ostrich feathers in her broad-brimmed leghorn hat, white gloves. You really cannot imagine how pretty she looked."
"You are quite sure she is not an angel droppea down here by mistake?" "Don't be cynical, Justin. •She's just a merry.l hearted girl, as human as she can be."

-Tnat's a contradiction, isn't it? T thought human nature was mean, and selfish, and cross.' "Oh, no, Justin, not at all. You are thinking of the' leavings' that were dealt out to you," and. she looked up into his face and laughed. "I do think I got more than my fair share of original sin," he answered. "But what shall we do with ourselves this afternoon?" "Oh, anything, so long as it does not require effort," she said, brightly. "It is too hot for violent exercise. Father says if the weather keeps like this harvest will be upon us directly." People who live in the country have to be con- tent with small things in the way of entertain- ments. Consequently they get into the way of entertaining themselves, and find pleasure in ways that never occur to dwellers in cities. To the blas6 City youth there may not seem much pleasure to be extracted from a tea-drink, or a country fair, or a village feast, or a ploughing match, or picnic on some grassy cliff by the sea. But country people know better, and it is to be questioned if rich and fashionable folk who pay to be entertained get as much pleasure out of theatre and card-party and dance as country people do out of the simple pleasures they manufacture for themselves. Justin and Dorothy spent most of the afternoon in the shadow of the orchard plantation, and time did not hang heavy upon their hands. When the sun began to dip behind the firs that crowned the hill they went out on to the cliff and sat down. It was fine to see the sun like a great ball of fire sinking into the ocean. Fine to sde the clouds take fire and burn blood-red down to the very edge of the sea. Fine to watch the shining track of light across the moving waters like a highway to the Celestial City. It was late when the Lovedays got back, and Justin had gone to bed, but he fancied he heard a sweet girlish voice singing an old love song just as he was dropping off to sleep. Perhaps he was mistaken; he was too sleepy to inquire. The next morning as he journeyed to Trelford he reflected that he would have to wait now until Sunday before his curiosity could be satisfied with a sight of Ruby Loveday's face. Friday was market-day, and he always got home late that ' evening, and Saturday was no better in that respect. It bad got to be the custom of people— though they liked short hours themselves—to keep shop assistants on their feet till nearly midnight. "But I shall see her on Sunday at any rate," he reflected., "I wonder if they will go with us to chapel? Not very likely, I fancy. I saw it stated in some paper the other day that the West End of London knows nothing of dissent. So most likely they will walk to St. lago, Churchtown, in which case they will start earlier than we shall, and, of course, we shall see them go." So the long and toilsome hours of Friday and Saturday wore away, and Sunday morning dawned at length, bright and cloudless. Justin donned his Sunday best, and giving his moustache an extra, twist, sauntered out into the orchard. Now and then he glanced surreptitiously over the thorn hedge at the front garden, and every time he did so he expected to see the vision of a dainty figure, clad in white, and of an exceedingly pretty face. But disappointment still dogged his steps. Mr.', and Mrs. Loveday came out into the garden, and wandered up and down for several minutes in animated conversation, but Ruby did not appear on the scene. He learnt later that she had got cold, and had been persuaded by her mother to stay in bed. "That comes of getting her feet wet," Dorothy said, sententiously. "I told her what would happen." "When did you tell her?" Justin questioned, with pretended indifference. "On Friday afternoon. We scrambled down the cliff together, and hunted for crabs in the p 0015.., You should have seen her. She was just wild with excitement, and didn't take the least notice where she was going. If the pools had been deep enough, she would have drowned herself, I verily believe.* . „ .

, John Pentyre laughed. "She's just as frisky as a young kitten," he said, "and a sight prettier. Ruby came downstairs to tea, but she did not venture out of doors. Justin was ready to bite his finger-nails with disappointment. He loitered in the orchard and in the lane outside the front garden, he glanced at the window of her bedroom again and again; he even made an excuse for going into the hall, which was now used exclusively by the Lovedays, but nothing came of it all. The one face that he was aching with curiosity to see, kept persistently out of sight. Mr. and Mrs. Loveday, as he expected, went to church in the morning, and in the evening they expressed a wish to go to chapel with the Pentyres. Justin had declared during the afternoon that he - - would not go to chapel a second time. Now he regretted it. He had missed a splendid opportunity of getting better acquainted with their guests, and perhaps of being invited to their rooms. "Just my luck!" he muttered to himself; but there was no going back on it now. Dorothy promised to stay at home to keep Miss Ruby company, and when Justin heard that announcement, he brightened up again. "The girls will know, of course, that I shall be in the house alone," he reflected, "so very likely they will ask me to keep them company. And ill they do—why, 1 shall not say no." After the elders of the two families had taken themselves off to chapel, Dorothy disappeared to keep Ruby company. Justin stationed himself near the door that opened into the passage leading to the best rooms, and waited somewhat impatiently for his sister's re-appearance. Now and then he heard a faint hum of voices, the low ripple of laughter, and he laid his book upon his knee, and bent his ear towards the chink of the door. It was a most undignified thing to do; but he was almost consumed with curiosity. , Later he heard a step, and he pushed his chair a little distance away, and took up his book again. Dorothy camo bounding into the room a_minuta later. "You here still ? " she questioned. "I thought you were going for a walk.' "I feel too lazy," he answered. "Besides, I did not know you were going to spend the whole even- ing with—that is, in the other part of the house." "Do you want me for anything in particular.?"'; she questioned. "Oh, no," he answered, indifferently; "and it is evident you don't want me." "Well, not now," she said, with a smile. "The fact is, Miss Loveday and I are having a splendid time. "So it would appear," he replied, and theix Dorothy disappeared again, leaving the door ajar. He tried his best to conquer his chagrin, and to become interested in his book; but it was a vain endeavour, especially as every now and then low ripples of laughter and snatches of conversation floated out to him. Then the piano was opened, and a few:firin chords were struck. "Dorothy is going to sing," he said to himself. The next moment the clear notes of a rich con- tralto voice seemed to fill all the house. "I hear thee speak of a better land." The words were as distinct as if he sat by the side of the singer. Justin sat like one spellbound until the song was ended, then he drew a long breath, and rose slowly to his feet. What kind of throat could a voice like that come from? he wondered. What was the singer like? "It is evident I am not wanted," he said to him- self at length, and he put on his hat and went out into the orchard. The next morning Mr. Loveday went off to London for two or three days, and Justin took up the burden of life at the stores. It was nearly dark when he returned On Tuesday evening, and he found the household in a state of consternation. Miss Loveday had gone out alone early in the afternoon, and had not returned. Search had been made in all directions, but no tidings of her could be gleaned. The last seen of her she was talking with Amos Blue in the turnip , field, and was then in the best of spirits; which way she went after that, no one knew, for no one had seen her since. Her absence was not noticed until tea-time ; but not turning up at the usral hour her mother got anxious, and that anxiety had deepened with every moment since. ( To be continued.) mere Sr

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. Lively Proceedings
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL. Lively Proceedings

A meeting of the Warrington Town Council wee held I on Tuesday evening. The Mayor (Alderman Roberrs) Presided and thore were also present—Aldermen Sutton, Prancemb, Heaton, Bolton, Monks, Hutchinson, Coun- cillors Tmnion, Shillcock, Wilkinson, John Evans, 8 Davies Bennett, Smethurst, A Jolley, William Roberts, John Roberts, 0 Plumpton, A J Jolley, W J Forshaw, W Broueh, L Ellison, Rogers, J Sampson, T B Wilkinson, with I L Whittle (town clerk), S Wilson (deputy town clerk), J Fairhurst (borough treasurer), Dr Gornall (medical officer), T Longdin (borough sur- veyor), J DSIC (sanitary engineer), J Sutcliffe (deputy borough surveyor) W H Grimsdale (electrical engineer), W S Haddock (gas engineer). The Electric Light. The Council Chamber was lighted for the first time by electricity, and the improved illumination wag the sub- ject of general comment. The corridors of the Town Hall are now also lighted by the new illuminant. The Mayor's New Year's Wish. The MAYOR said that before proceeding with the ordinary business of the agenda might he again, and officially, wish every member nf the Council a very happy and prosperous new year ? Might he also take the opportunity of congratulating the Town Hall, Park, and Baths Committee upon the excellent result of the illumination to-night, and also the Electric Lighting Committee, through the Chairman and the Deputy- Chairman, upon the success which had attended their efforts up to the present. (Hear, hear.) Finanoe and Estate Committee. Payments on Account of Contracts. At a meeting held on December 10th it was resolved that in order to avoid delay in the payments on account of contracts, the Borough Trev.urer be instructed to Prepare a supplemental schedule of the amounts certi- lied by the respective engineers to be passed at the first meeting he'd after the receipt by the Borough Treasurer Of Such Certificates. Alderman Seem GREEN said he understood that it Was the desire of the General Purposes Committee that the matter of the auditors' report should be taken now. Alderman BOLTON said that the matter should be dealt Wtth when to minutes of the General Purposes Com- taittee, who passed the resolution, came forward for !PProval. Alderman Snew GREEN proposed the confirmation of 'he minutes. Alderman MONB3 seconded, and it was agreed to. Watch Committee. -

Tbn MAYOR Rrowled, and Alderman Sugrox seconded the confirmation of these minutes, and it was agreed to. 'fhe minutes included resolutions te the effect that the resignation of Detective Delahav, be accepted, he having been appointed a Detective Officer in the Rhodesian Constabulary, and, that 15 be Riven to Detective Dslahay as a present on leaving the force ; resolved also that the Council be recommended to join the Lancashire Inebriates Acts Board, and that Mr. Aldermen Heaton be apnointed the representative of the Corporation on the Board for the year 1900-1901 ;:and that members of the police force under 35 years of age be required to attend gymnastic drill at the Gymnasium. P.C. Marsh has retired on the ground of infirmity and been granted the maximum pension, viz £BO 12s. 'Street Improvement and Lighting Committee. Alderman SUTTON proposed the adoption of the minutos end alluded to the renaming of several streets

by the committee. They bad reverted to the names originally applied to the localities with the object of ke-ping before them the ancient history of Warrington, though some of the names were not euphonious. It had been pointed out to the committee however that a com- plete plan of enumeration had been carried out and to alter the names at present would cause confusion and trouble to the ratepayers. He thought it advisable that the questioe should be deferred therefore and proposed the minutes with the exception of the one relating to the renaming of streets. Counciller BENNETT seconded and the minutes were Passed.
Health Statistics.

The minutes of the Health Committee were proposed for confirmation by Alderman Sutton who stated th the birth rate for 1900 was 36.7 against 38'07 in 1899. the death rate 19 4 against 20.9, zymotio death rate 2'7 a„,gainst 5.01, infantile mortality 162 against 194 in 1899. ?taken altogether the figures showed a v ry satisfactory 214Provernent. (Hear, hear.) The MAYOR seconded—Carried. Sanitary Works. 4 Proposed by Alderman Monks, seconded by Councillor °l„;,n Evans, and passed. , the minutes contained a resolution that the tender of r George flolford for the supply of slops at 8s 6d /mob Do accered, and that the tender of Mr Harry Fair el(mgh tor the erection of a public urinal near the Central station, at £B5 12s 7d be accepted. Level Crossings in the Streets. Alderman Hawroa moved the confirmation of the minutes of the Paving and Sewerage Committee which 'contained the following resolutions ; That the White- cross Company, Ltd, baying given notice of their inten- tion ti construct the tramway or level crossing across Priestly -street as sanctioned by the Council in 1888, the Committee offer no objection provided that the agree- ment of the 23rd of April, 1888, be complied with ; that the tendet of Messrs. Clare and Ridgway to supply 1,000 tong of setts be accepted. The ALDERMAN mentioned that the committee had also ace^Ptbd tenders for street-making to the extent of Councillor WILLIAM ROBERTS referred to the applica- tion of the Whitecross Company and said he thought it Very impirtant proper regard should be paid to the safety of the passers-by. A short time ago he had a very narrow escape from death by an engine which Vdenly crossed Milner-street on the level crossing there. 'An warning WBB given. The MAYOR : That was in direct violation of the tette of the agreement, and the Company have since Riven their assurance that those terms should be strictly agreed to. Councillor BENNETT asked what the terms were. He NClui opposed to level crossings under any circumstances. Councillor SAMPSON said he thought a flag was always Waved. The MAYOU ; They are not allowed by the agree- ment to send an engine across the street at all. Alderman Surrne referred to the fact that the agree- ment was .dated 1888. He thought it was desirable that they snou'd have a reconsideration of the question as Warrington now was much different to Warrington in 1885. Councillor TINNION said he believed they had the Power te do away with any such crossing on giving three months' notice. Councilor PLIMPTON said the traffic in the street whore the tram way was desired was three or four times as great as in 1888. Ho could say also from his own ob- servation that the Coancil had not acted according to the agreement by any means. The engine often went across Milner-street, with sis or eight tracks behind it. The mason said if the Company desired to consider the 'Whole question afresh it could do so by giving notice. Alderman HEATON said there were about seven or eight crossinms in the town beiaz worked under the same agreement. He thought sufficient precautions were taken !I Prevent any accident. Having granted the Crossings .0 some works they could not refuse others. The MAYOR thought the conditions Stringent enough tO safeguard the public. Alderman HEATON gave an assurance that the regula- tions should be enforced and the minutes were passed. COUNCILLOR SIIILLCOCIK. Oa Councillor SHILLCOCIC vcondiag the minutes of the School Attendance Committee, the Mayor expressed the pleasure of the Council at seeing him back again. (Applause). Councillor Srumcocs thanked the Mayor and Council for their kindness and sympathy with him in his recent bereavement.

NEW CEMETERY REGULATIONS. pouncillor Joais EVANS propos3(l the acceptance of the Minutes of the Cemetery Committee and alluded to the new table of fees, charges, and regulations, which he Said was simpler and more equitable than the last. They bad ceased to charge ld per letter for lettering on grave- Stones, and several suggestions from the masons were bong considered. Councillor WiLiiiisom seconded.—Carried.

WANT OF HARMONY BETWLEN COMMITTEES. The Pulling up of Streets.

Alderman FRANCOME —prodosed the minut,s of the I Water Committee one of them being a resolution that the Paving and Sewerage Committee be requested to furnish a monthly list of streets intended t 3 be formed and paved. Alderman HEATON proposed an amendment that this minute be rejected. He contended that they gave three distinct notices to everyb Councillor TINNION seconded the amendment and I remarked that he thaught all the committees and officials of the corporation might work more harmoniously together. Alderman Sarrox thought the resolution desirable If it would lessen the pulling up of streets by different committees to the surprise of everybody. Alderman M4)NICS said he had been of the opinion for some time that there was friction between the officials and he suggested that all the officials of the Corporation should mect every fortnight to discuss corporation affairs and arrange matters so as to prevent this pulling up and laying down. He thaught it in the best interests of the town that something of the rort should be arranged. The Mason said if the Paving and Sewerage Com- mittee acceWed this resolution by the Water Committee they put upon the latter committee the full responsibility for breaking up streets. Such things were disgraceful and put the Paving and Sewerage Committee in an unfair light. He thought that by accepting the resolu- tion they would put the responsibility, on the com- mittee which failed to carry out its proper work after notice had been given. Alderman HUTCHINSON : I should like to see " a blending " of the Committees. Alderman FRANCOMS said he thought it scandalous that Committees should break up streets unnecessarily. If this request being complied with would prevent the Water Committee breaking up new streets, the Paving and Sewerage Committee ought to be glad to agree to it. A vote was then taken and the amendment lost. The minutes as proposed by Alderman Francomb were then confirmed. Councillor TINNION : We shall rub it in in future. (Laughter). The Thomas Morris Shield.

The minutes of the Gymnasium Committee were pro- poses by Councillor TINNION, who referred to the reso- lution that in grateful appreciation of the services ren- dered to this institution by the late Mr Thomas Morris, a subscription Shield be provided, to be called "The Thomas Morris shield," for competition by the public elementary school children of Warrington attending the Gymnasium. He said a memorial tablet was first thought of. but they finally decided on something which would further the gymnastic instruction of school chil- dren. The shield would not become the absolute property of any one school,but the names:of the winners each year would be inscribed upon it. They did not make it a begging business, but subscriptions would be thankfully received. Councillor W. ROBERTS seconded, and said they could not perpetuate Mr Morris's memory in a more accept- able manner. If any man took an interest in the youth of Warrington it was Thomas Morris. (Hear, bear). The minutes were confirmed.

div.head: Electric Light.
div.p: The Electric Light.

Alderman Mowxs proposed the —acceptance of the minutes of the Electric Lighting Committee and re- marked that it looked likely that they would be able to complete the new electric lighting station for about £2.000 less than was estimated. (Armistiee.) He expressed the thanks of the committee to Mr. Gricasdale and the staff for enabling him to fulfil the promise he made before Christmas. The minutes were passed.
A BELATED AUDITORS' REPORT.

div.head: Why it Was Withheld. Alleged Extravagance.
div.p: Why it Was Withheld. Alleged Extravagance.
The Mayor Threatens to Close the Meeting.
HEATED DISCUSSION.

" —•- • -- At a meeting of the General Purposes Committee held on the 31st December a communication was read, signed by 25 persons as members of the Ratepayers and Pro- perty Owners' Association and others, the text of which and the committee's decision was published in the " Examiner " last week. The auditors' report on the accounts of the Corporation for the year, 1899-1900 was read, and it was resolved: That the chairman of the Finance, &c., Committee be requested to bring the same before the Council at the next meeting; that the Mayor be authorized to purchase a plot of land at Longford, containing 19 acres 2 roods and 21 perches, for the sum of £l,lOO, and that the Town Clerk be authorized to apply to the Local Government Board for their sanction to the borrowing of the sum of £7,000 for the alters, tions to the existing baths and the erection of new Turkish baths. The Meson. I have to move the confirmation of the minutes ef the General Purposes Committee. Alderman MONKS seconded. Alderman SHAN'T GREEN said he begged to introduce to the Council the report of the auditors in accordance with the resolution on page 17. After he had read it he shoukl be prepared to give some reasons which influenced the Finance Committee in declining to give its sanction to the incorporation of the report with the abstract of the borough accounts. Alderman Green then read the report as follows : Warrington, 27th duly, 1930. To the Mayer, Aldermen and Burgesses of the Borough of Warrington.
Dear Sirs,—

Borough Audit. We have pleasure in reporting that we have completed our audit of the accounts of the Corporation for the year ended 31st Merck, 1900 Including the accounts of the Gas and Water Departments and Parr Hall. The duties of borough auditors, up to the time of our last report, were limited, according to the best authorities to the actual verification of accounts which had been sanc- tioned by the,various responsible committees. Their scope however, has been extended by the subsequent decision of the Court of Appeal. in Thomas v the Corporation of Devonport, Whereas Mr Justice Phillimore considered the simple vouching of the receipts and payments the whole duty of the auditors, the Lord Chief Justice, In the Higher Court, says that they are bound to ascertain, amongst other things, whether the payments are duly authorized and legal. We notice that certain expenditure in connection with the recent Borough Bill has been provided for out of the Walker UM Fund, Instead of being charged upon the rates. We are of opinion that the manner in which the Middleton Scholarship has been desit with is not legal, and that the interest from the bequest, instead of being accumulated, ought to have been at once applied to the purposes indicated by the will. We think it our duty to call attention to the large amount which is annually expended upon deputations. and to the increasing disposition towards extravagance in this matter; and we notice that the Corporation sub- scribes to many voluntary associations and societies, and sends large deputations periodically to attend their meet- ings. The expenditure under both these heads wants care- fully watching. and there are other items in which a judicious economy might be practised with advantage.— Faithfully yours, (Signed) ARTHUR BENNETT (Chartered Accountant), Mayor's Auditor. Joan HARRISON, JAMES BOLTON, F.S.A.A„ Elective Auditors. Alderman Strew GREEN proceeded to defend the action :1 i c teisee Finance Committee in not publishing the report. i7e d Twobroefetghhet beforematters the he Council.referred o Ito hnaedLa el r epaadyy been specially . ment of a part of the costs of promoting our Bill in the House of Commona,and the7other the Stla2(.9. inn that the enebreourselyeeleetfet to dfethe Corporation etheeherttim by e r necessary . a l i d d te e- st ou nm should so g make up, by the addition of the interest, the round figure of £l,OOO. On the 4th January, 1893, the sug- gestion with respect to the " Middleton Bequest" re- ceived the sanction of the Council, and on the sth Sep- tember, 1899, 1 gave a full explanation of the circum- stances and of the transfer from the Walker gift account of this particular item. Wnat possible benefit, therefore, could be gained by bringing these two questions up again it was net possible to conceive. Then we have a referenee to the question of the audit, and the duty and responsibilities of the auditors. Opinions differ, even amongst the judges, as to what these duties and res- ponsibilities really are, but no such difficulty arose here. We have for years treated our elective auditors in the most liberal way possible, EVERYTHING HAS SEEN OPEN TO THEM, every facility afforded to them, and I venture to say few towns have so thorough an examination of their accounts, or, I think, have more confidence in the ability and integrity of their elective auditors than we have. Why, then, should they go out of their way to burden their report with this. I can Certainly suggest something better. If the Mayor's auditor, who is a member of the institute of Chartered Accountants, will send it to the Council of that body and urge them to get the House of Commons to amend the law making the duties of accountants and auditors clear and comprehen- sible, something yet may be done, for it is well under- stood that that association is the stumbling block in the w ay of Parliamentary action. (Hear, hear.) With reference to the last item, there was probably some ground for introducing it, and if it had stood alone most likely no objection would have been taken to it. Even in this, however, they had no monopoly. Several mem- bers of the Finance Committee bad been seriously con- sidering the question, and they had taken out the figures at considerable trouble. I do not think this was known to the auditors, but I want the Council to under- stand that these gentlemen, anxious for the good reputa- tion of the borough, wanted to know what we were spending. The very expression " A Corporation depu tation " has about it an unfortunate ring, and has become suggestive of extravagance. Well. Mr. Mayor, it was discovered (and I think you will conclude there was very little to complain of) that the COST OF DEPUTATIONS bad for some time past averaged about £250 per annum It is a fact that the number of professional and other associations with which our officials are connected in- creases, but these associations at their gatherings give to

their members the very best and latest information. We must also remember the increasing importance of our engagements and the increase in the number of our officials and the responsibility that we place upon them, so that I do net tbink we ought to object either to their membership or to thole attendance at the gatherings of their associations. It is of the utin ost importance that our offioials be well equipped, not behind our neigh- bours, and they must be abreast of the times. We want from them the beet service that can be obtained, and it is for us to see that their equipment is as perfect as it can be. It has also been our custom to send with them one or two members of the Council, and I think this is wise, for in ordinary business the directors of every ire- portant commercial undertaking would do likewise. But these are net all. We must not forget the necessary journeys and interviews with other important governing bodies, their plant, their management, interviews with the Local Government Board and other officials, so that I think you will agree with the members of the Finance Committee that we are not spending much more than we get value for. lam of opinion, therefore, that the Council will conclude after this explanation that the Committee acted wisely in declining to permit this docu- ment to be appended to and form part of the accounts. These accounts are sent over the country, and I ask now whether it would have been consistent with the dignity or helped to maintain the reputation of the borough if It had been. I am not saying that there may not be many things that the auditors could at times wisely bring to our notice,but I strongly object to the inteoduc- then of matters of this simple kind in the report, which should be an important one. The Mayon : The matter is now before the Council if any member wishes to say anything. ALDERMAN BOLTON COMMENDS THE AUDITORS. Alderman BOLTON thought a mistake had been made in trying to cloak anything, although he thought the auditors only did what they considered to be their duty. They were paid to examine the accounts, and they went out of their way to make an addition which did not apparently suit the Finance Committee or members of the Council. Alluding to the Walker gift, he said it was never intended that it should be applied in the manner it was applied. The money ought to have come out of the expenses of the Water Committee. But that was all over, and he thought the auditors might be exonerated and thanked for their courage in running contrary to the opinions of the Finance Com- mittee. If the auditors had given a garbled report which suited the Finance Committee, the report would have been published. What was there to cloak? The auditors had only done what they thought was right, and it was not for the Finance Committee to pass a vote of censure on them. The Council and the public ought to know what the auditors had done. "FINANCE COMMITTEE HAD COMMITTED A GRAVE ERROR." Councillor Timm observed that he could not held thinking, after hearing the report, that the Ficiance Committee had committed a grave error in suppressing the report as long as they had done. There would have been considerably less newspaper correspondence, con- siderably less suspicion in the town, if the report had been brought before the Council immediately after it had been received. Be did not say that it should have been published as part of the accounts, as the Chairman of the Finance Committee had explained, to be sent all over the kingdom, because there were many things ki the report, which probably had not been dealt with in the most accurate way by the auditors, but he was very pleased indeed to find that they had auditors in the borough who were quite prepared to do their duty. H e should like to get to know really what was the duty of the auditors. A good many people seemed to think they had gone far beyond what the law required of them, but he could not see that there was anything in the report that necessitated it being kept back so long, (Hear, hear.)With regard to the Middleton Trust it was for the lawyers to say what was to be done with the bequest and it was for the Council to be guided by the Town Clerk whether the action the Museum committee took was strictly correct or not. He did not think the auditors were the best people in the world to judge whether the thing was legal. He would naturally go to a lawyer or to a solicitor before he would go to an accoun- ant. As to the Walker Gift Fund, he thought the ref erenc to it was perfectly justified. He did not know anything that had been done by any committee that had caused more just criticism in the town than their action in reference to that matter. Alderman SHAW GREEN • It was not the committee's action. Councillor TINNION I blame those who initiated the policy. Continuing, he said, he was given to under- stand that it was undesirable and almost illegal to charge the fued upon the ordinary borough rate, and no doubt it was charged on the Walker Gift Fund, because it was the easiest way of dealing with the expenditure at that particular time. He objected to that course being adopted at the time, and he still held the same opinion. The next matter was an important one,namely that of the cost of deputatioue. He had been of opinion for some time that they had had probably not too many deputations, but too large ones, and be should like to say in reference to the remarks with regard to the volun- tary associations that they as a Corporation suiscribed to, and to which deputations went, that he considered the money spent in that direction was very well spent It had been said that they could get the result of the meetings of the associations, and quite as much inform- ation as they needed to have about them, from the printed reports which were published, but he wished to put the matter in this light, and in a light which some people seemed to overlook and for.zet. Every borough official in the kingdom, every member of a corporation, every district councillor and every representative of other governing bodies went to make up these essocia- tions, and if the whole of these people stayed away there would he no meetings at all. There would be no papers read, no information given—(hear, hear)—and the officials and the members of the Corporation would not have an opportunity of learning. Be had been on deputations himself, and he ventured to say that when he returned to Warrington and discussed the matters Which had been under Consideration with the various committees with which he was connected, he had been helped to come to a just and to a right conclusion as the result of what he had heard at the conferences. (Hear,

hear.) The Mayon: That is not strictly relevant to the sub- ject under discussion. The question under discussion is the criticism of the auditors on the cost of the depute. tions. Alderman Shaw Green has stated that that state- ment in the report is not true—that there has not been a tendency to increase the amount spent on deputations. ' Councillor TINNION : [did not say that. The MAYOR: I am saying that you are now discussing the value received, and that is not relevant. Councillor Trtmrox : I still submit that they raised. the question of the legality of the expenditure. The Miavon : No. They say they notice a growing tendency to extravagance in this and other directions, and it is not a true statement, as is borne out by the Chairman's own figures. I have no doubt that that is what the auditors intended to convey, but it is not true. Councillor ItxtrioN : What lam trying to show is that the money that has been spent-- The MAYOR: Has been well spent. Councillor Trxmom : Has been well spent, and that the officials and members have received great benefit and that the town through them has received a benefit from the money spent. ALDERMAN SUTTON "A BIT SURPRISED." • Alderman SUTTON quite agreed with the opinion that it was not advisable at any time to withhold the audi- tors' report, and he was therefore glad that it had been read that night by the Chairman of the Finance Com- mittee. He thought that the explanations which had been given were very fair. In regard to the deputations, he had always been of opinion that the Corporation spent a lot of money on them, although it had not been mis-spent, and they derived a valuable advantage. He had always found that those members of the Corpora- tion who had complained most about the cost had always been ready and eager to attend with the deputations whenever they had had a chance of doing so. He was a bit surprised that, as an auditor, Councillor Bennett should be a patty to calling attention to the cost of the deputations when he hisnself had been--

div.head: IHE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, JANUARY 11, 1901
div.p: IHE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, JANUARY 11, 1901

portion of the cost. If his conscientious scruples were so much oppose,d to the colt of the deputations he won- dered why he did not refuse to go on the ground that there was no necessity to do so and that the expenditure was altogether too large. As the Council knew, they had by a recent resolution decided not to send more than two members as a deputation. He cornidered that the sum they spent was a reasonable one in comparison with the cost to other cerporatioos. At all events, as he had shown,it was not desirable to withhold the report of the auditors or anyone else b c:sause there was a section of the public which was always disposed to consider that there wag something wr)nte, and that information was being withheld for a purpov. He thought now every- one must be convinced that the Corporation had no such purpose. Alderman Snavr GREEN I don't believe it. AN:demean SUTTON proceeded to state that they had considered the matter at a meeting of the General Pur- poses Committee the other night, which was equivalent ta a meeting of the whole ef the Council, tad had also passed the resolution which appeared on page 17, that the auditors' report be brought before the Council, and that was in answer to a corn nunication signed by 25 persons as members of the Ratepayers and Property Owners' Asaociation. He, therefore, did not see the necessity of further going into the matter and repeating what was said on that occasion. Be thought that the resolution which had been passed explained itself and was a complete answer to those gentlemen who were desirous of considering the matter in a fair spirit and accepting it as the only answer which could be given to them. Be was sure there was no one connected with the Corporation who had a desire to keep from the ratepayers ' anything connected with the work of the town. (Hear. hear). He for one would only be too glad if more rate- payers would take an interest in everything connected with the Corporation which was for the benefit of the Iratepayers. He did not think there was any necessity to discuss the matter further.

div.head: TUE FIRST BREEZE.
div.p: TUE FIRST BREEZE.
Councillor SMETHURST (interrupting) : I think that is out of order, Mr. Mayor, and is a personal remark so far as Councillor Bennett is concerned. Alderman SUTTON: I am not making a personal
remark. The ale You : I must rule you out of order, Councillor . •

_ Smethurst. Councillor Bennett signed this memoran- dum and is personally responsible for the statement it contains, and it is quite relevant to the issue that Alder- man Sutton should show if he can, that Councillor Ben. nett has been inconsistent in criticising actions to which he himself has been a party. Councillor Smarnuesr : There has been a great deal of inconsistency at this Council. The MAYOR . I can bear no more. ALDERMAN SUTTON AND COUNCILLOR BENNETT'S CONSCIENTIOUS SCRUPLES.

Alderman SonroN, continuing, said be did not make these remarks in any personal spirit, but Councillor Bennett had only been too eager to go on deputations ("No, no ")—and had sent in his bill and had added his

div.head: WORDY WLIIIPLBII
div.p: WORDY WLIIIPLBII

COUNCILLOR BENNETT WITHDRAWS. Councillor BENNETT : I may have some reason to differ from the worthy Alderman who had just spoken, with regard to something he has said about myself. I think that some of the opinions expressed and the interrup- tions which have taken place are extremely uncalled for and demand a reply from me. The Mayon: Do you mean something I have said to- night?. CoBrICB N lOT BENETT replied in the affirmative. The MAYOR (warmly) : Than I must ask you to with- draw, or I shall not allow you to proceed. I interrupted Councillor Smethurst who was calling Alderman Sutton to order, and I decided that what the Alderman was saying was perfectly relevant, and I gave a reason. I have done nothing more than that. Councillor BENNETT : You oractioally accused me of telling an untruth. The MAYOR: I did not. I said that if Alderman Sutton could prove you were inconsistent in having made a report which criticised the action in which you had taken a part, he was perfectly within his rights. I expressed no opinion. Councillor BENNETT : My impression will scarcely tally with that. IThe MAYOR: You withdraw your statement or I close the meeting, Councillor BENNETT : You said the statement was un- true. _ . _

The MAYOR : I decline to bear you. Councillor BENNETT : It is consistent with your con- duct on two previous occasions. The MAYOR : I decline to hear you. The statement is not true. I did not interrupt ; I simply expressed an opinion as re the relevancy of what Alderman Sutton was saying. I did not express an opinion whether what he was saying was correct or net. Alderman SUTTON : I was only stating a fact. The MAYOR (to Councillor Bennett) Are you pre pared to withdraw ? I should be sorry to close the meet. irdz, but I am not going to be accused of partizanship. Councillor BENNETT : It is not an accusation of partizanship; it was a statement of simple fact. You said the paragraph in the report was not true. The MAYOR : I said so, and I say it still ; but what has that to do with the question of procedure ? Councillor BENNETT : I say I resent it. The MAYOR: You can prove in your own way that my statement is not correct, but don't accuse me of making a deliberate mis-statement. I won't stand it from you or from anyone else. Councillor Barmen' : That is not my intention. If that is what you complain of I withdraw It. The MAYOR: You have a perfect right to prove your own case. Councillor Bexisexy : And that is all I want. If you close the meeting I shall not have an opportunity of doing AO. The MAvon : If Ido it will be as a protest against your assertion about me, which is not correct. If you withdraw the statement go on by all means. Councillor BENNETT Theo I withdraw it. I think you have introduced a certain amount of heat into the discussion which is not necessary. The MAYO 2 : I snail not allow you to reflect on my conduct in the chair. lam invested with a certain amount of authority, and I will try to carry out my duty fairly, and I hope as courteously as human frailty will permit me to do. You are within your rights to prove your case to the hilt, but don't put in my mouth words I have not uttered, and attribute to me a state- ment I have not been guilty of. Councillor BENNETT : I have not done so, and if I have I withdraw. I contend that I have done nothing of the kind. It is no use personally pushing the matter forward. I hate these personal altercations and attacks made on me personally. That is all I wanted to say. Alderman SUTTON: Can you deny you have attended deputations ? Councillor BENNETT : You said, Mr. Alderman, that I bad shown a considerable eagerness to attend deputations I desire to deny utterly that I have over done so, and during the seven or eight years that I have been a member of the Council I have been on probably fewer deputations than any other member. As fa* as I remember I have only been on two or three during the whole of that time. Alderman BOLTON said he had been on fewer still. "SUSCEPTIBLE TO THE CIIARITS OF A GOOD DINNER.' Councillor BENNETT! I give:you the precedence. I have been once to Liverpool, once to Preston, and once to London in about eight years, and I think that it will compare very favourably with the record of any othe r member. Ido object to being taunted with anytmager- nese in going on deputations. Some of the members may be susceptible to the charms of a good dinner, but it is not a form of temptation that pirticulatly appeals to me. Alderman Simms' ; Who are you referring to ? Councillor BENNETT You accused me, and I strongly object to it. Proceeding, Ceuncillor Bennett remarked that if the Finance Committee had given the report in the first instance, as they ought to have done, none of this burly—burly would hays arisen. Last year they had considerable difficulty ever a similar matter. The com- mittee then chose the middle course, and if they had chosen the middle course this time the public would have accepted it. Alderman Shaw Green said it would not have been wise to publish the report with the general statement of the accounts, which were sent all over the country. It was, however, not necessary to do that. If Alderman Shaw Green had published the report with the minutes of the Finance Committee it would have come before the Council, and the people of the town would in due course have been made familiar with it and the " bogey" be raised would never have occurred. The report was really a very innocent and harmless document, and it only proved that unnecesary concealment led to suspicion, engendered bad feeling, and did more harm than good. Be hoped that in future the committee would publish the report whether with the accounts or not. It was felt very strongly that that should be done. The onus rested with the Finance Committee, and now after six months' hesitation they had come over to what the auditors thought, and had done What they said ought to have been done.

TILE AUDITORS HAD BEEN ABUNDANTLY JUSTIFIED by the result. If an accountant was worth his salt he would not take instructions from anyone—(hear, hear) —but would take an entirely independent view of matters coining under his notice. They were, of course, not perfect, even chartered accountants, Alderman Shaw Green—(laughter)—but they exercised their judgment to the best of their abilities. If the public did not like it they could appoint other elective auditors, and the Mayor had his remedy too, tut so long as they held the position they might take it from him they would do their duty without regard to what any individual or committee might do. Referring to the duties of auditors be said they could not afford to ignore such a pro- nouncement as that given by the late Lord Chief Juice. He agreed that the law was very unsatisfactory in re- gard to the duties of accountants. That, however, was the highest legal opinion available at the time. AMATEUR LAWYERS. ' •

--- Personally he was not prepared to take the ipse dirit of an amateur lawyer who criticised them in preference to the opinion of the Lord Chief Justice. His opinion herd the field for the moment. The paragraph in regard I to the expenditure in the Borough Bill was, he thought, most desirable. They knew the matter was referred to in the House of Commons and excited very scathing comment from the committee who sat to consider the Bill. It excited very great feeling in Warrington at the time, and they (the auditors) considtred it their duty to the ratepayers to bring that prominently before them. The illegality in connection with that had been purged by the money being taken from another source. With regard to the Middleton scholarship their action did not rest merely on his opinion. He had consulted a solicitor, and he had said that their (the auditors') interpretation
