of the clause was perfectly right. The Toni CLERK: We cannot accept lawyer's opinion here. Councillor BENNETT Then you must take it as an amateur lawyer's opinion. Proceeding he said probate of the Middleton will Wild issued six years ago. In 1897 one third of the residue, £953 8s 61, was paid to the Corporation. lc, was decided by the Museum Committee and afterwards ratified by the Council, that the money should be allowed to accumulate until it reached £l,OOO. He agreed on that occasion. He had not thought of it in its legal bearings at that time. Wnen he came to go into the matter in detail as a part of his duty as Mayor's auditor, it was brought prominently to big notice. He considered it his duty to look into it. He rcad the will carefully, and came to the conclusion that technically the way in which the fund had been dealt with was not legal, and a good cage might 148 made out of it by a gentleman who was not an amateur lawyer to prove they a ere right. The result had been a substantial injustice. The fund was not invested until a short time ago.
-The MAYOR That was :not the fault of the Corpo- ration.

Councillor BENNETT : Whose fault was it ? The MAYOR. I should not like to say. The money did not come into the bands of the Corporation until Decem- ber let, 1897. :Councillor BENNETT Slid that was so. It had been in the hands of the executors three years before that. During those six years the young men of the town had not been reaping the educational value for which the money was left. They had suffered a very substantial hardship, though the committee might have been well- intentioned ire what they did. The committee decided that the £950 should be accumulate i at 5 per cent per annum until it reached £l.OOO and the first scholarship was not granted until a little before last Christmas. For three years the young men of the town had been en- titled by every principle of fairness and justice to share this advantage. Alderman SHAW GREEN: Two years. Councillor BENNETT Well then, I will say two years. It is unfair that some young men have been debarred from a privilege. The MAYOR: Will you mention one? Councillor BENNETT : Mr. Dell is one. The MAYOR: You have not mentioned Mr. Bolton's son—your colleague's son. Probably that had a good deal to do with this report. Councillor Smarr : Mr. Bolton's son succeeded in winning the scholarship last year.

The Maros: It is a curious coincidence. COURCiller BENNETT : Justice is the same all the world over whether it is Mr. Dell's son, Mr Belton's son, or Mr Roberts's son. Continuing, he said he was not going to have his conception of justice limited by personal con- siderations. Not only WAS it illegal on the grounds of law, but on the grounds of equity it was unjust. The last paragraph in the report was a matter of opinion,and It was doubtful whether it was necessary for the audit- ors to express the opinions they clod about the deputa- tions, but it came fairly within their discretionary power. They must be judges of their own duties and bear the responsibility. At any rate they were on the right side and gave the note of warning which was very much needed, and one result was a resolution limiting the number composing deputations, and their work had not been altogether fruitless. To bring the matter to a conclusion, he would repeat that the state of the law was exceedingly unsatisfactory, and no one would be more delighted than himself if it were better and more clearly , defined, but, pending any amendment of the law they were bound as auditors to do their duty to the best of their ability under the present conditions. They had endeavoured to do so, and he thought the town would feel that they were justified in the matter. (Hear, hear). *4Councillor PLUMPTON said he wished to ask a question If the Council was going to vote on the matter. The MAYOR said there would be no vote. Councillor PLUMPTON said the Chairman of the Finance Committee had said that he was not responsible for this report not having been brought before the Council. Who was responsible? He thought that had caused all the trouble. If the auditors' report had been published at the time there would not have been this trouble. THE MAYOR REPLIES. The MAYOR in reply, said the only answer he could give was that he was afraid the Finance Committee were responsible for the non-publication of the report. No one regretted more than he did the non-publication of the report, as he expressed himself at the last meeting of the General Purposes Committee, and suggested that the report should be brought forward by the Chairman 'of the Finance Committee that night. It was his sug- gestion, and it was in order that this criticism, which be contended was unjust, uncalled for,—and in some measure impertinent, might be properly replied to. NOW WAS THEIR OPPORTUNITY. It would have been far better if that reply had been made at the time the report was 'presented to the com- mittee. There was no question that the suppression of this report bad been misunderstood outside and had lent a certain colour to the somewhat scurrilous and abominable insinuations which had been conveyed to the press by ctrtain persons in the town who would be better employed in looking after matters more directly concerning themselves, and in regard to which there was room for considerable improvement. In regard to this criticism he wished to introduce as little heat as possible, but members of the Corporation who desired to do their duty honestly, honourably and justly must resent the insinuations con- tained in the report. In the first place the reference to THE EXPENDITURE UPON DEPUTATIONS was in his judgment—though of course his was only the opinion of a layman, but was worth as much as that of Mr. Bennett—he said without hesitation that so far as he was concerned it was outside the scope of the duties of the auditors. No deputation was sent by the Corpora- tion without first of all receiving the sanction of the committee and afterwards the sanction and support of the Council. While the somewhat enlarged view of the duties of elective audi•ors was a very proper and correct thing to take as a guide, they must remember that the statement of Lord Justice Russell was not part of a judgment, but part of a dictum, and must only be taken as a part of his dictum. (Hear, hear.) The law advisers to the Municipal Corporations Association state that the words of the late Chief Justice must only be read as applicable to cues of illegality of an obvious character. Secondly, it was not for the elective auditors to set themselves up as lawyers and decide what was legal and what was illegal, but if anything of an obviously illegal character came under their notice it was for them to bring it to the notice of the committee. Ile thought that Coun- cillor Bennett was going to prove that the remark he (the Mayor) made to the effect that the statement was incorrect that there was a tendency towards increased expenditure in regard to deputations, was untrue. He bad, however, said nothing about It. In the face of what the Chairman of the Finance Committee said,that the average annual expenditure for the last few years had been only £250, he (the Mayor) said with all respect to Councillor Bennett, who would be this last man to make a deliberate misstatement, that the statement was riot correct.

THE EXTENDITCRIS HAD NOT INCREASED. On the contrary, there had been a distinct tendency to decrease the expenditure. Throughout his mayoralty in the past year there had been far less money spent by him in representing the Corporation at various places than had been spent by any of his predecessors for many many years. Re had curtailed the expenditure in that direction, and it was :partly because it had been inconvenient to him, being a very busy man, to spend much of his time out of town. He resented very strongly,and he thought it was perfectly reasonable to expect that members generally would resent the insinua- tion that there had been a tendency to be more extrava- gant than formerly. The statement was not correct. Dealing with the THE MIDDLETON TRUST.

the Mayor said the probate was proved in 1894. The money left under the will for the establishment of schol- arships did not Come into the possession of the Council until the Ist December, 1897. Why it did not come to them before that time it was not his business to Say. He had too much respect for the memory of the dead to attempt at this stage to suggest that there was any reason except a proper one for the delay on the part of the executors in handing to the Council the money due under Hut will. The fact was they did not get it before then. They were in no sense responsible for the delay which occuired between 1894 and 1897. They received the sum of £953 us 4, and the committee had to con- sider, as this money had to be invested, what was the best thing to do in order to perpetuate the greatest possible value in respect to the scholarship founded un- der the trust. They decided as business men, that it would be better to lay it aside to accumulate until the capital sum had reached £I,OOO. In coming to that de- cision they did what they were bound to do. They took the host legal advice obtainable for their assistance. They consulted the Town Clerk. He took time to con- sider the matter, and finally advised them that the step was perfectly legal. Ile (the Mayor) did not think any one would deny that it was far better for them to make the perpetual value of this scholarship as great as they could rather than invest the smaller sum at once for the sake of one or two youths whose interest et how- ever, they had quite as much at heart as Councillor Bennett or the other auditors. The trust was for the whole of the children of Warrington. It was the duty of the committee to make the best of it. That was the sum and substance of the offence for which they were criticized. Cauneillor Bennett and he and others in the room understood perfectly well the terms legal and illegal, but in the feverish state of the public mind as it existed at the present time reflections of this kind upon the action of the Museum Committee were seriously mis understood, and such suggestions to certain minds con- veyed the idea that the committee was morally as well as legally responsible. In men of strong sensibilities, such as oneself. The reflection was resented very warmly, as be resented it, and the criticism of the auditors was regarded as UNJUST AND IMPERTINENT The committee had been justified in their action by the fact that the whole case had been submitted to one of the Charity Commissioners, and he expressed himself perfectly satisfied with the action of the committee.

(Hear. hear.) Ha (the Mayor) preferred the legal opinion of the Town Clerk and that of the Commissioner as to the legality of their action to the dictum of the gentle- men who had appended their signatures to the auditors' report. He thought be had proved that the remark about the illegality of the committee's action was ill-timed and uncalled for. He also thought he had shown that the remark about extra vagance was not just nor was it true. As regarded the question of

div.head: WALKER GIFT_
div.p: THE WALKER GIFT_

everyone knew the circumstances. The committee en- trusted with the conduct of the Bill on behalf of the Cor- poration were unfortunately made responsible for certain acts d )ue utterly without their knowledge or consent by certain agents employed. That conduct was brought , before the notice of the committee in the House of Commons. The committee, expressed its opinion in no unmistakable terms regarding the conduct of those officials, and the representatives of the Corperation gave the committee an assurance, as they were hound to do, that the expense of that part of the Bill, which they considered an improper expense, would not be charged upon the rates. It was not charged upon the rates. If there was any crime in charging the amount upon the Walker Gift Fund the Council, as a whole, and not any Individual members, were responsible for the offence. He talk it that this was one of the very things for which the Walker Gift Fund was intended. There were similiar wiestions of expenditure in connection with all public bodies. There was the " Nemo " fund in connec- tion with the Board of Guardians, which had existed for years and years, and was used for purposes not necessarily of an immoral character. He resented as strongly as any man any suggestion that any member of the Corporation had knowingly lent himself to such practices. The whole of the circumstances he had re- lated, painful as they were, and they were especially painful to those who had to face the ordeal of the criticism of the House of Commons Committee, were dealt with at the time. They were within the knowledge of the public of Warrington as they were published in the press. What, therefore, was the necessity for re-opening such an unpleasant question on the part of the auditors ? There was such a thing as consistency. Reverting to the Middleton trust, the Mayor went on to say that Councillor Bennett was present at the Museum Committee's meeting when it was decided to allow the interest of the sum to accumu late; he took part in the discussion and was a party absolutely to the decision of the committee in reeard to the manner in which it was proposed to deal with the fund. Mr Bennett might be able, like a character in a celebrated novel, to assume two characters, one as a member of the Corporation and of the Museum Coma- mittee, and the other as an auditor of the borough. (Laughter.) He (the Mayor) hoped he himself would always be consistent as an individual, as an ordinary ratepayer, and as a member of the Corporation. Councillor BENNETT . Excuse me interrupting have you never changed your mind ? The MAYOR Sometimes. (Laughter). Either Com- Ciller Bennett was right when he agreed with the rest a the members of the committee in deciding that this Interest should accumulate for the purpose of increasing the perpetual value of the scholarship, or he was right now. At any rate it would have been far better and fat more agreeable if they had had the benefit of the legal advice of that eminent adviser at the time the Museum Committee, was trying to come to an honour- able and fair decision rather than in the form of a critic- ism which only suggested to the "man in the street ' that there was something not only illegal but immoral. He was glad this matter bad been thoroughly thrashed out. _
r, but

Councillor PLIMPTON rose to speak, when Alderman MITCHINSON remarked that they had heard enough, and left the Council Chamber. The minutes of the General Purposes Committee were then pat to the Meeting and carried. No comment was made on the decision of the committee regarding the request of the Ratepayers and Property Association to inspect accounts.

div.head: SAD DEATH OF AN ARMY PENSIONER.
div.p: SAD DEATH OF AN ARMY PENSIONER.
Discreditable Conduct of a Witness.

Early on Saturday morning the body of a man, who subsequently transpired to be John Walsh, an army pen- sioner, formerly connected with the 85:h Regiment (foot), aged sistT-seven years,was found in an 011t!101.198 at the rear of 33, Brick-street. He was in a sitting posture on the floor, and his coat was drawn over his head, as if to keep himself warm.—The inquest was con- ducted at, the Police Station on Monday evening by Mr. S. Brighouse, County Coroner. The Coroner informed the jury that about nine o'clock on Friday night deceased went into the Lord Rodney public-house. The landlord, however, saw that he was under the influence of drink, and refused to serve him. He left the premises, and went with two men named Higham and Edelsten into Higham's house. He there drank a gill of whisky, and about 10A5 sent for half-a- gallon of beer. Deceased was in such a condition that Mrs Fligharn refused to let him stop. Higham and Eines- ton took hi tu and left him in an outhouse at the rear of Brick-street.

Dr. Smith, police surgeon, said he made a post-mortem czamination of the body. The right lung was much congested and was practically useless. The heart was slightly diseased and the liver was fatty. Death was due to failure of the heart aided by congestion of the lungs. Exposure to cold would hasten the man's death. Ada Middleham, 10, Laarence-street, Earlestown, gave evidence of identification. She said deceased had lodgei with her for four years. Ha was 66 years of age and was an Army pensioner. He left her in September, and she next saw him dead at the mortuary. James Higham, labourer, 1, Banner's yard, said that on Friday night about nine o'clock he went into the 'Rodney and deceased came in. The landlord refused to serve him, and Walsh asked him (witness) to get some whisky. The deceased, himself and a man named Elles- ton then left the place. They went to witnesa's hdbse ar.d had some whisky: About 10.45 deceased sent his wife for some whisky, for which he gave her 3s. After drinking some deceased vomited and witness's wife re- fused to let him stay in the house. They took him to the outhouse and left him there.

P.S. Barnett said that abut 5.50 on Saturday morn- ing he received information that a man had been found in a closet in Brick-street. He proceeded there and found the deceased on the fllor. Life was extinct. He found on searching his clothing, an old knife, a tobacco•box, and a few buttons. There was no money. His Army papers showed that he bad just drawn his pension, which was £3 Oa sd.
The Corona; (to Higham) : Can you give any explain tion to the jury of the fact that there was no money Lon him P Witness : I eannot.

The Coroner: At nine o'clock he bad a sovereign. Witness I gave him the money back. He added that the men was in the Rodnoy from nine o'clock in the morning till nine at night drinking with women. The Coroner: We are not talking about that. We are talking about this sovereign. . . _ . .

William Ashman, night-soil-man, 25, Leicester-street, spoke to finding deceased. Be said be tried to waken him but found that he was dead. Be then gave inform- ation to the police. In answer to the Coroner, Ashman said he was sitting on the floor. His coat was over his head and his trousers were drawn up to the knees. The Coroner said it looked very suspicious for them to take the man to this place, which was very secluded. Why did they take the trouble to take him down a street ? From nine o'clock to 11.45 deceased had 20s in his posSessiou. Be had no money when he left Higham's house. Higham : I gave him the change. fie gave Mrs Higham 33 and told her to keep the change. The Coroner : Where did the 15s lid go to ? Higham : He paid for several gills or pints of beer. The Coroner said he thought the evidence of Higham should be taken with a grain of salt. He did not be lieve that he had told the truth. They had heard what was the cause of death. The jury had to decide whether the deceased died from exposure or not, and wnether Higham was deserving of censure.? . .

The pery after a short consultation returned a verdict to the effect that " Death was due to exposure," and considered that Higham should be censured. The Coroner in censuring Higham said his evidence was unsatisfactory. He bad seen his police record. He could not say that he honestly believed he had told the truth,

COMMERCIAL PAM:MRS.—According to " Kemp's Me cantile Gazette "the number of new Bankruptcy pro- ceedingsfin England and Wales gazetted during the week ending January sth, was 58. The number in the corres- ponding week of last year was 57. showing an increase of 1, being a net increase in 1901, to date, of 1.
Personal.

At the recent examination held at the Royal Academy of Music, Miss Florence Tuft, of Warring- ton, was successful in obtaining her diploma of Li- centiate for pianoforte playing, Miss Tuft is the first local candidate who has obtained the distinction.

The Rev E W Lummis, M.A. of Hull, has accepted the pastorate of Cairo-street Church, which was rendered vacant by the resignation of the Rev W H Drummond, who several weeks ago accepted an appointment at Belfast.. Mr Lummis, who will come to Warrington with exceedingly good creden- tials, occupied the pulpit of Cairo-street Chapel, twice in November and twice in December, and his earnest and powerful discourses were listened to with attention and earned for him the respect and esteem of the congregation generally, The Chapel Committee recommended that he be invited to accept the pastorate, and Mr Lummis, having given the invitation careful consideration, accepted it. lie is the author of several well-written books, and A may be interesting to note that he is on the list of University extension lecturers, and was at one time in orders in the Church of England. It is expected that Mr Lummis will enter upon his duties in War- rington about February 100,

div.head: NEW CENTURY. Sermon by the Lord Bishop of _ Liverpool.
div.p: THE NEW CENTURY. Sermon by the Lord Bishop of _ Liverpool.

To celebrate the dawn of the new century a special service was held in the Warringtou Parish Church, on Thursday last week There was a large oily regation, which included members of the Corporation, who had attended at the invitation of the Mayor and the Rector. The Mayor (Alderman Roberts) was present. Owing to illness the Rector was unable to take part in the service I which, in his absence, was intoned by tie Rev A S Cameron,theleSeuns being read by the Revs E J Willcocks and Canon Penrhyn. The preach ,r was the Lord Bishop of Liverpool (the Right Rev. Dr Chavasse) who based an eloquent discourse upon the words " For their sakes I sanctify myself." St. John xvii, 19. He said that no thoughtful man or woman could pass from the old cen- tury to the new without feelings of the deepest wonder and awe, To pace the old familiar landmark on the shores of time, to pass out of the century in which they had been born, in which their immediate forefathers had lived, and with whicb all their memories were asso- ciated, and to 'enter upon a new century veiled as it were with mist, and containing untold possibilities, must impress the imagination and I touch the heart. A great and good man had recently said that the feelings uppermost in the heart of the ' Christian must b?. those of confession, thanksgiving, and aspiration. Of confession to God for their sins as indi- viduals and as a nation; of thanksgiving for the mercies which they had received. Wailst war had ravaged the fairest plains of the continent, England had been saved from its ravages ; whilst the most ancient thrones had been shaken, the throne of Eogland stood to-day un- shaken in the hearts of the people ; our liberty was unimpaired, and the nation was undivided. Of aspiration, for before them there lay a magnificent future, in which, by the grace of God they and the country might play no mean part. How could they as individuals, do their duty to God and to the country in the new century which had just dawned upon them? He believed the words of the text " For their sakes I sanctify myself" unfolded it to them. To-night at the beginning of a new century, he appealed to them to sanctify and consecrate themselves for the good of tbeir fellow men. The England of to-day, was worth main. taming, and expanding, was worth brightening, and if they were but true to their calling, English Christianity and civilisation ought one day to compass the whole earth. Let them follow in the footsteps of their Master and be willi og to separate themselves from all that was debasing and sinful, and by self sacrifice seek to make the people in the town or county in which they lived better, happier and holier. He looked back upon the century that was passed and history told him what was the condition of the working-classes at the beginning of the century, and his experience told hint what was their condition now. They themselves knew better than he did, the vast advances which had been mado in the last seventy years in the matter of education, housing and even of temperance. Let them seek to carry on these advances so that when the New Century closed their children's chil- dren might be able to look back and bless their memory and thank God for what they had been permitted to do for their happiness. They were to-day what the past had made them, and they were to-day helping to mould the future of their race and their country. As followers of the Crucified, as inheritors of this magnificent hiller!. tance, which had come down to them through God's mercy from their forefathers, he repeated to them the saying of the Divine Founder of their religion " For their sakes I sanctify myself."

div.head: Concert in Thelwatt Mission.
div.p: Concert in Thelwatt Mission.

A successful concert was given in the above MiSei Mon the other evening by several locid artistes Admiral Jones Parry occupied the chair, and there was a large audience. The artistes were Miss Arm- strong (soprano), Miss Collin (contralto), Miss Day (violinist), Mr S Hassell (tenor), Mr G H Gough (bass), Mr H Sinclair (banjo), and Mr E Sanders (humorist.) A capital programme was submitted and the various items were well received, especi- ally Mr sander's contributions "The Liverwing Testimonial" and "Hew Bill Adams won the Battle of Waterloo."—On the motion of Mr A M Prescott, to Nelson, seconded by Mr Wastener, of Whitmins- fer, a hearty vote,of thanks was accorded the concert party for their service.

S URELY thera is A Strange Anomaly. nothing more signifi-

cant than that this country should begin a new century full of ideas.. of what must be done to revitalise our institutions 'with a Conservative Government in Office. For the past fifteen years we have been under the sway, more or less, of Conservative rulers and majorities, and we have been slipping back to re- action at a considerable pace, alike in education, taxation, and general politics. A new century arrives, new competitions are threatening, new fears are generated,and yet we have nothing better to fall back upon than a Government with a , majority obtained on a false and temperary issue, and which has exposed us to the severest strain. the Empire has had for fifty years, we might al- most say for a century. It is an aucenaly that should impress the thoughtful, no matter west their general polities may be. We are not re- quired to protect our institutions against revolu- tionary changes. The claim is that we shall go forward and renovate our institutions, and enter with confidence upon competitions in commerce, science, administration,and knaval and military de- velopment. Itis not a claim limited to one political party. The surveys of the past ceutury,the forecasts of the future,have been all tinged with expectancy and with forebodings. We have no confidence in our ability to hold our ow a unless we make great changes, and they are demanded with a courage and a breadth that make our position uncertain and precarious. If the country had confidence in itself and in its rulers, in the general principles upon which our Attire are being conducted, it would hardly be so clamorous, so exigeaut, so in- clined to be gloomy. The Government of the day, however, is animated by old principles, and it is in the hands of men who have spent tueie lives in resisting wholesome changes, iu keeping back democratic sentiment, and in preserving the weight and power of aristocratic classes and pri% lieges. The House of Lords is still unre- formed; the Church of England is becoming more Romanist and sacerdotal ; national educa- tion is hindered in response to ecclesias- tical preferences; Federation is proclaimed to be a virtue in our Colonies, but an evil at home; and tee dominant party has iniscalculeted over a war, allied itself with an obstrurtive trade-interest, and rewarded support- ers with doles out of the public exchequer. What real hope can we cherish that the new century will begin well for us under these conditions ? Great Britain is regarded as a progressive country, and its statesmonanave usually been alive with gener- ous impulses, and responsive to popular ideas. Can it be said that Lord SALISBURY'S Administra- tion is the one best fitted to cope with the new problems and to re-invigorate our institutions, to develop the Empire, to meet the threatening com- petitions ? It can do what it likes in Parliament, because it has a subservient majority in the Commons, and a permanent majority in the Lords. No Liberal Government has ever been in this unique position. But it has had men of ideas in it, men who do not see the highest wisdom in the man in the street, and men who had not lowered statesmanship to a series of electioneering tricks. There has been more respect for the generous and progressive tendencies of the people. The new century begins with a British Government which is giddy with the effects of Colonial patriotisin,and is absolutely without any other progressive idea. It is full of dodges, and they are of the electioneering type only. Lord SALI,d3 Tray never has any enthusiasms. and so we canieit expect them to animate his colleagues. Place arid power are the two great aims of the Conservative party; and so we enter upon a knew century—a century of generous ,easpirations and great ideas—with a mediocre Conservative Ministry presiding over our destinies. It only adds to the sadness of the situa- tion if we are told that it is the only possible Government under tho circumstances.

English Catholics are Engli•h Catholics and the Temporal Power. supposed to have acquiesced in the aboli- tion of the Temporal Soveroignty of the POPE. The English Government has certainly done so,and no thought has troubled the public mind of any

possible restoration. Accordingly, the passage about the Temporal independence in the address of the English pilgrims, read and prepared by the DUKE of NORFOLK, is a great surprise. The address referring to the new century said: "W -, pray and we trust that it may witness the restoration of the R man PONTIFF to that rosition of Temporal independence which your Holiness has declared : necessary for the effective fulfilment of his world- wide charge." The pious hope that the _reunion ' of Christendom may soon take place, and bring , with it the gathering of British Christians into "one fold and under one shepherdis nob half so striking ' as the passage we have quoted, if it reveals what are the hopes which animate British and Irish * Catholics, and, to some extent, the advanced Ritualists of the Church of England. The Temporal independence of the POPE has passed away with the assent of all the European Powers, and Italy has played her part in bringing about its discontinuaace as essential to Italian unity. If English Catholics are now united in anxiety to restore the Temporal Sovereignty they are placing 6 themselves in an awkward position, not only with ' regard to their own Government, but with regard to Liberal opinion throughout the world. The POPE as King is one thing; the POPE as a Spiritual Read ot an ecclesiastical organisation is another thing. Even good and strong Protestants admit that he has rights as the latter, but they cannot be expected to accept him as the former, or to lend any encouragement to the view that restoration is wise, convenient, or to be worked for in harmony With existing constitutionalism. The Drain OF Nonrorx went to]Sorith Africa, it was said, to show the Papal journals of Rome that a good Catholic I could be a British patriot, and that the , cause of the Boers, as advocated in those journals, Was not accepted by British Catholics. How : Would he have been placed if the POPE, as Sovereign, had espoused the cause of the Boers, and commanded Catholics gener- ally to render them assistance? His own Prayer amounts to a confession that under auch circumstances he would - have obeyed the Roman Poxravr and been disloyal to the British Governmant. If it does not mean as much as this it is merely a pious opinion. At any time under a King-Pope national loyalty might be put to a severe strain, and then one or the other would have to give way. It is explained that the passage we have quoted was inserted in RDMO, under direct or indirect Papal inspiration. We cannot accept the explanation as improving the position of the British Catholics who composed the pilgrimage or who remained at home. The pilgrims either honestly believed in the wisdom of re- storing the temporal Sovereignty or they did not. If they did, have they not in ade it imparative thi, patriotic Catholics at home should make a pro nouncement of sympathy or dissent? If they did not the proceeding shows the unwisdom of British Catholics allowing themselves to be influenced in expressing their opinions by Roman intrigues. In either case an unpleasant situation is restored,and the old controversy is revived at a m3st inconve niont time. Papal Sovereignty and modern Con- stitutionalism cannot be reconciled, if plain logic be employed, and the less laymen have to do with the subtleties of ecclesiastics the better. The Duke of NORFOLK is a British patriot, approved and tried, but his hankering after Papal Sovereignty reduces hie moral dignity and intellectual stature consider- ably in our eyes.

Loyal Canada has a grievance against the pire at large. It complains that an altogether erroneous conception is held of the climate of the greater part of its territory. The inapression is all the more deep and lasting as the poets have done much to spread it. Mr Kipling is one of the chief sinners. His description of the colony as "Our Lady of the Snows" was bitterly resented at the time as tending to convey the idea that Canada, on account of the severity of the weather, is utterly uninhabitable during a considerable portion of the year. Other poets have followed suit, but it appears that it was reserved for one of the Lord Mayors of London, who was no poet, to be re- eponsible for the deadliest insult of all, in the 'representation of Canada by a Polar bear! It is contended, on the other hand, in a pamphlet Which the Canadian Government has just issued With the view of enlightening the public in the Mother Country, that even in the North-West the climate is superior to that enjoyed by most coun- tries. Tile cold in the severest seasons is of a dry character which makes it positively exhilarating, and the sunshine in the depth of winter is so glorious that it is positively delightful to open the doors and windows, though the temperature of the suter air is forty or fifty ,degrees below freezing Point. There are no blizzards, and the whole ,seowfall of the winter hardly ever exceeds eighteen , inches. It might further be pointed out—if any- thing more was needed to dispel the popular mis- conception of the North-West Territory as a -frozen, sterile land—that its climate is probably ( almost identical with that of the regions in Asia which modern science, with little hesitation, fixes upon as the cradle of the human race. ~ --- 'While red-tapism is strongly to be deprecated , in the distribution of patriotic funds for sufferers by the war, and while it is admitted that inquiries r` into the private affairs of beneficiaries may be carried too far, it seems desirable in the present ill' state of public feeling to remind advocates for • .reform that some sort of scrutiny into the claims of applicants is absolutely necessary. In this .respect the pension roll of the United States offers '. .5 useful object-lesson. Thirty-five years after the • close of the Civil War this roll'keeps on increasing, ' 'end, though it now contains nearly a million ,ames, it certainly will keep on increasing until means are 'found of checking the corrupt practices i Which have lately been laid bare. It actually appears that there are in being pension attorneys, 1 who have formed pools, and, in one instance, a ' ?regular trust for the manufacture, collection and elivieion of bogus pension claims. Their method of operating is described as consisting of the Ilk- in,g of a few negro women who can neither read nor write to present claims as the widows of dead soldiers, whose names have been obtained from cemetery headstones, and a few ignorant nev,ro men to play the part of old 1 soldiers. Of course, neither men nor women claimanta know what amounts have been obtained , , on their applications, and are accordingly given What well satisfies them, while the pool distributes 1 . the rest among its members - and that this is a profitable business is evident'. when it is stated that in one ease, which was the subject of a prosecu- tion, a pension attorney obtained arrears of 4,000d0i for ac old coLured woman in the back- woods, and generously gave her 75d01. for her share of the plunder. We do not suggest that corruption emild flourish to this extent in this ,country. Our purpose iG merely to point out that those who oppose the new scheme of the Patriotic Fund Commissioners as likely under existing cir- cumstances to stop the fount of charity are on aurer ground than those who merely object to the incluieitorial methods of distribution. ---- Few societies anywhere nave made such quiet bUt sold progress ae the Warrington 'Anglers Association. Progress was the leading note of the snnual report of the Society and its position amongst the Izaak Walton fraternity may he gauged by the fact that there are 464 meinoers. It is dietinctly a workingman's organkation, but at the head of affairs there are some men of posi- tion and business aptitude who are lending their influence and assistance, in order to make the '''')ciety of greater usefulness and worthy of the (‘ i? ' t ~ , , igii
co, le- cal sts Icy in )at tgo sin in les
an !t- -lab )at ,nd Or-

town. There are few angling societies in such a happy position as that enjoyed by the Warrington Association. Like other institutions it has had its days of difficulty and anxiety and even last year there were some dissonsio:u which seemed to bode ill for the Society's welfare, but fortunately these have been healed and there is every pros- pect of the future history of the Association being still more prosperous. Those who are interested in the welfare of working men will be well-wishers for the success of the Society. The following of the pis- catorial art by such a large number of workingmen cannot but be a step in the right direction. To 'get away from the smoky and grimy town for a few hours for the purpose of lingering beside Ipleasant streams and babbling brooks, even if the , 'catch" is insignificant, is infinitely preferable to sitting in a dingy pub on a Saturday afternoon. Instead of a membership of 400 we should be glad to hear of twice that number being associated with the Warrington Association in the forth- coming season.

"Life's little worries " are often spoken of and written about now-a-days, and they by no means unmerit the attention bestowed upon them. There is one which troubles the whole of mankind at the present moment, and that is the difficulty of writ- ing 1901 instead of 1900. Habit is a wonderful thing and there is something remarkable about the way in which one's usually obedient pen per- sists in cleaving to the old and familiar 1900 in defiance of calendars and the indisputable fact that a now year and a new century have both begun. "The pen is mightier than the sword" we are daily told, and it may almost as truly be said just now that the pen is mightier than he who wields it. 'Tis absurd that one's serious thoughts should be disturbed by an erratic pen which seems deter- mined to perpetuate an era dead and gone. We ' viciously crossthe offending cipher out and feel almost inclined to rail at the endless cycle of years , for daring to "cycle." Consolation of the ' sweetest kind comes to each individual, however, when he receives missives from his acquaintances bearing the last century's offensive and officious date. Great and small alike are victimised by the pen which will -its own way go, and the only cure is the cause—viz time.

The agitation which is being fostered in War- rington with the object of compelling an investiga- tion into the Corporation contracts and accounts shows no signs of diminishing, and while there is little evidence, as yet, proving anything to be seri- ously wrong, facts are being unearthed and deduc- tions made which it will hardly be in the interests of the Council to ignore. Recently we have had before us the letter of a correspondent drawing attention to the fact that a membr of the Cor- poration is chairman of a committee which has allotted a fairly large contract—over t6oo—to a recently-formed local company in which he is also a large shareholder. And at a subsequent Council meeting the same gentleman moved the acceptance of this tender among other minutes of the committee, and it was passed. Looked at superficially these facts have a very unsatisfactory appearance, but an explanation has been voluntarily given us by the gentleman implicated, and we may say that it is of such a character as we are, ourselves, incline to accept. Nevertheless it cannot be denied—and it is not denied lay the person most concerned —that he has, unwittingly we are ready to believe, placed himself in a most anomalous position. Sus- picious people can easily place a black interpreta- tion on such evidence and many of them are naor.. than willing to do so. This case may be the fore- runner of others not so easily explained an it behoves the Council to take every precaution that its dealings are above suspicion and thus be able to meet a challenge with a clear conscience. For ourselves, we believe that the Council may be trusted to act straight forwardly and openly at the proper time.l

div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT.
A Provincial Letter.

--- In the provinces the use of salt for getting rid of snow on the footwalks, or in front of houses and shops is deprecated, and in some cases forbidden, by the local authorities. But the new borough councils in London order these things differently, and have during the week themselves resorted very largely to the u e of salt for clearing the streets of the snow, that appears to have been falling every- where. What the effect may be upon the public health may become a matter for future considera- tion. This has yet to be seen- But if no ill effects are reported we shall expect the London example to spread to provincial towns, and to possibly find imitators even in the town and urban councils. Pickled shoe leather is not comfortable or desirable in other resp:cts.

Scarcely a week passes without its record, in the local or other paper, of a fatality of the "didn't know it was loaded " order. This week it comes from Devonport, where one of the " boys " of the training ship Lion shot another, bespattering his brains about the place, and the usual plea was offered. It would be rude, of course, to point a gun, whether loaded or unloaded, at one of our legislators, but until something of the kind happens it appears useless to expect any legisla- tion on the subject, much as the necessity for it has been urged in the press, and by more than one of our Recorders. Instead of the consequences in each case proving deterrent, the evil seems to increase, and accidents" to multiply. If the public could I be favoured with a return, showing the number of fatalites resulting from the pointing of fire-arms-- always, of Course, in play, idiotic as it may seem,— it would astonish most people There is all the more reason why the " pointing" of any loaded or unloaded weapon should be made punitive in the 'encouragement now given, for national reasons to accurate shooting, and the more general handling of the rifle, and in the establishment of rile clubs.

Hitherto the consecration of part of a cemetery has been compulsory, the law courts mandamusing, Banal Boards which refused to ask the Bishop to I consecrate. But, under the Burials Act which has just come into operation, the authority " may, if they think fit," apply for consecration Their dis- cretion, howev,sr, is not absolute; for if satisfied that. a reasonable number of persons desire conse- cration, and are " prepare I to pay the consecration fees, the Home Secretary may apply to the Bishop to consecrate.

--- There appears to be much annoyance in some of the school board districts where rhe by-laws have been adapted to the new requirements of the Board of elducation. Those who are immediately affected do not as a rule rush into print with their grievances, and for this reason, perhaps, are assumed not to resent the most recent curtailment of their privileges, which in many cases means that children able to earn their own living at thirteen years of age shall not be allowed so to do, because they have not passed a certain standard under the Robson Act. In the old days, we are remin led, it was considered the object of education to fit boys , for earning their own living. But these people need to be told in return that whey, was good for the old days is not, by common consent, good enough for the new, and that ir, will pay better in the long run to keep well up in the race of pro- gress, than to lag and waste breath by complaining of the pace.

A great difficulty is experienced in connection with some School Boards t know how to deal wit", habitual truants At one T uant School, that need not be mentioned, after much local agitation on the question ot corporal punishment, this kind of chas- tis-ment was abolished, and for a little while there was not much to complain of in regard to th con- duct of tie children. But it appears that since the latter began to realise that n effective influ-lr,e was likely to be brought to bear, things have become as had as they well can be, and although , flier, is n-t disposition to revert to corp -tral punish- ment, the metnh -rs are at their wits' end to know what else to sugg at.

There is no connec jot between Truant Schools and Hooliganism, of COUCSO, as r g i'ds the revived controversy on flogging; although ihero are those who have alleged that there is some connection between ir egular attenda me at s diool and Hooli- ganism, which seems rather far-fetched. But the feeling is becoming increasingly prevalent that it is necessary for th- arm o• the law to be lengthened or strengt on • d if the con net of many brutes and

div.head: EX/tYIINER, PRIDAY, JANUARY 11, 1901
div.p: THE EX/tYIINER, PRIDAY, JANUARY 11, 1901

uffians in our midst is to be ,:ffac uallv dealt with and improved, Judges, magistra.es, coroners,grand juries, ani others have been lifting up their voices to demand the extended application of c3rporal punishment for divers offences which it seems to be well nigh impo sible to repress by ordinary pr iven. tive or punitive means. In other words, the lash or the "cat "has again come to be recommended for application to the backs of wife-beaters, violaters of women and children, assailants of the police,and all ruffians who culpably employ violence, stopping , short of murder. The time is believed to have come 'when an Act of Pan l ament should be passed, mak- ing a judicious select ion from the foregoing list, or embodying the whol ; of it. for wholesome purposes of correction. Theru is, perhaps, a danger that in this highly educated age, we may grow highly sen- sitive as well, and this is what to all appearances, and according to a strong body of public opinion, we are coming to, with the result that in our thickly populated towns, brutality and ruffianism in their varying forces will gain the mastery over us. Every day the papers, in most parts of the provin- ces, are full of sickening reports of crimes of vio- lence,usually visited by absurdly light punishment. very many of these cases, the innocent victim has been made to suffer more severely than the ruffianly assailant is allowed to. When the latter has been caught and fairly brought to justice, which it is needless to say, does not always happen; whatever the super-sensitive among us may say it must be admitted that there is here a balance needs adjusting.
VISIT OF THE LOSTOCE GRALAIK MINSTREL TROUPE.

The great attraction--a.t—tl-ii Mersey Mission to seamen on Wednesday night, was the advent 01 the Lostock Gralam Minstrel Troupe. Mr Wilshin Murch the president of troupe the took the chair, and referred to the valuable work such an institution as the one they were assembled in could accomplish for the social betterment of the sailor. Toe troupe it appeared was composed of working men many of them natives of Runcorn,and this gave their doings an added interest. The first part of the entertain- ment was taken up with the circle. Mr J Stubbs acting as interlocutor. Excellent musical items followed and the whole concluded with an inimit- able farce" The Demon Gramophone" the char- acters in which were ably sustained by Messrs W tubbs, J Booth, Walky and Smallwood.—The accompanist was Mr W Boden.—At the conclusion of the entertainment Mr W Show proposed and Captain Crowther seconded a hearty vote of thanks to the troupe for their kindness in coming over. SONS OF TEMPERANCE, RUNCORN. The usual meeting of the above Order was held on Saturday night in the Green way-road School. There was a good attendance. A number of members and officers from the Weston Division paid a fraternal visit. Mr Thomas It Whyte occupied the chair, and the newly-elected officers I were installed by Mr Thomas Cook, P.G.W.P., in an ' impressive manner. The newly elected Patriarch or Chairman (Mr Thomas fleesom) presented Brother Whyte, in the name of the division, with a beautiful emblem framed and mounted, containing the following resolution --" The Order of the Sons of Temperance, Life-boat Crew Division No. 195. Resolved, that the best thanks of this sub-division are hereby tendered to Bro Thomas It Whyte for his valuable services for three terms as worthy Patriarch. (Signed) Thomas Heesom, Patriarch; James Johnson, Financial Scribe." Mr Daniel Bis- brown said Mr Whyte during his tenure of office had served them well, with credit to himself and satisfaction to the entire membership. They all had a profound respect for him. He was a consist- ent and loyal member, and they hoped that his life would be spared for many years to continue this labour of love. Mr Thomas Cooke spoke in appre- ciative terms of Mr Whyte's services to the Order, and the following gentlemen also gave short addresses :—Messrs Alfred Noden and Thomas J Holt. Mr Whyte feelingly replied, thanking the brethren for their kindness. He had been con- nected with the Order for 18 years, sad it was never more dear to him than now. He was trying to do what he could for the cause. He would treasure their gift as an heirloom. (Applause). Messrs Daniel Kirkham and John Brown, of Weston, gave encouraging addresses, referring to the steely growth of tee division. BOY CRUSHED TO DEATH AT Vir/DNES.

On Saturday at the Moss Bank Hotel, Mr. Brighouse, County Corner, held an inquest touching the death of Joseph Griffiths, who was killed on Thursday morning. Inspector Strickland and Ser- geant Ratcliffe represented the police, and Mr. Webster was the foreman of the jury.—Thomas Griffiths,l9, Moss Bank-road, said he was the father of the deceased and that his boy was fourteen years of age. Ile had been working at Sullivan's works for the last twelve months. Witness was a plumber at the same works and his lad worked as a labourer for all the plumbrs. On the morning in question witness was not at work, as he was not well, and he told his son when he went out to inform the foreman. He had seen the cylinder which had killed his bay the day before. It was out of the way. He had to go to the lead pot for the strips. About ten feet from where it was propped up was a lot of lead. Some of this lead deceased had to take the lead pet to make some strips. He must have caught the prop that was propping the cylinder up, and he must have shaken it in some way so that it had fallen on him.—Asked by the Coroner whether he considered the pan safe when he saw it and was working at it. witness replied in the affirmative, but thought there might be per- hapa some safer way of supporting it in the future. —John Hughes, foreman, said he saw the lad alive about 10 15 a.m. He sent him to the workshop to make some strips of lead, and he must have gone to get the lead from some that was near a cylinder, which weighed three quarters of a ton, and which was being repaired in the shop. It was supported by a wedge similarly as it was at the present time. Witness saw it at 9.30 aud it was then all right. The pan would remain standing after the prop had been removed. There Was no one in the worksh Dp at the time the accident happened. The prop was between his legs when deceased was extricated.— The jury found a verdict of accidental death, and the foreman, Mr. Webster, suggested that there might be better means of preventing the cylinder from falling, either by running it against the wall or suspending it from a ceiling.—Mr. Minton said they would do all they could to prevent similar occurrences.

div.head: -..111..-. THE PRICE OF MILK.
div.p: -..111..-. THE PRICE OF MILK.

Local Farmers decide to Combine. A meeting of those interested in dairy farming was held in the Corn Exchange,Blue Bell Inn,Elorse- market-street, Warrington, on Wednesday evening, when Mr James Sadler, secretary of the Cheshire Milk Producers' Association spoke on "Some Aspects ot the Milk Trade;' with a view to the con- sideration of what steps should betaken in the way of corporate action. There was a large attendance. Mr Marsh presided in the absence of Mr VT Ben- nett, of Padget°, who had promised .£5O towards starting a local association if a hundred members I joined, each contributing El. In the course of a few remarks, the Chairman urged those present to combine in one body in order that they might be able to improve their position. Mr. Sadler in the course of his address said milk- producing and milk-selling was a business, and it ought to be a profitable business. That the ordinary market price obtained by the producers was too low needed no argument, whether they considered the rental of a dairy farm, the cost of working it, the coat of good dairy cattle, or the price paid for I milk by the consumer. From whatever point they , regarded it,milk-selling was not to the farmers the profitable business it ought to be. The only ques- tion was how they could best increase the margin 'of profit. They could not get cheaper labour, they could not get farms at lower rents in view of the great competition there was for them, and they could not reduce the cost of keeping Cows. There was therefore, nothing to be done but to increase the price of milk, arid for this purpose farmers must band themselves together. They could do nothing single-handed. The Cheshire Milk Producers' Association had been in existence for two years, and had already done good work. On their own admission, it was more difficult now for milk dealers to buy low-priced milk in Cheshire, and the Association wanted to make it altogether impos- sible.—( Ap please). The Staffordshire and Derby- shire Associations had an agent in London whose business it was to sell milk for members. This agent had only been appointee a few months, and had already earned his salary in the better prices obtained for the milk of teose he represented, and in preventing milk being sold below a certain defi- esse price. They might usefully follow the example lot these associations and have their agents in Man- chester and Liverpool. If necessary the association might even undertake the distribution and sale of milk in these cities. They had tried the experi- ment, a year ago of arranging a minimum price with the Manchester milk dealers, but he regretted to say tnat the Manchester milk dealers very soon repudiated the agreement. What was needed was an agreemant among the producers themselves. —(Hear, hear.) Another neceasiey to sacc issful working was some method of dealing with surplus milk, so as to prevent the periodic ii flooding of the milk market. Last summer he recommended some members of the Cheshire Association to make cheese for a time rather than sell milk. Those who took his advice did so greatly to their own advantage and the ad- vantage of those who continued to sell milk To do this on a large scale it would be necessary to have factories, and a committee of the Cheshire Aesocia- den was now considering the matter from that point of view. It might be asked why in the case of milk they should attempt to interfere with the ordinary law of supply and demand. The answer was obvioue for milk differed from other kinds of produce in having to be disposed of at once. It might also be asked whether, if they succeeded in controlling the supply of milk and in raising the price to a satisfactory level, there was any need to fear foreign cempetition. He would have been glad if he could have given an emphatic answer of R 3 to that question; bet he very much feared that foreign competition in milk was possible—in fact, he was not sure that it did not to some extent exist now. There was there- fore need that they should act cautiously and with moderation. Moreover, did it not occnr to them, if in addition to the many difficulties they had to meet at present, they one day found themselves face to face with tile new difficulty of the foreigner try- ing to take the milk market from them, that it would find them b Atter prepared to cope with this possible evil if they had organised themselves into a strong compact body and prepared to adapt them- selves to newlconditione,(Heo,thear.)ln working the Cheshire Association it bee been found impossible to have one set of prices for the whole of the area covered. What would be a good price at Whitchurch or Drayton or even in his owl town of Naetwice, would not be regarded as a good price by Warring- ton farmers, who had the advantage o' bein nearer the markets, This difficulty was being met by the formation of local committees to advise the Central Council of the special circumstances of each district. Mr Sadler afterwards discussed the pies. tiers of variations in the quality of milk. He said , that at present there was no legal standard for milk; each local authority fixed one for itself. He did not himself attach a great deal of importance to the giving of a legal standee I. The only true standard, in his opinion, was the cow it- selF, and he was glad to say that was the istaedard adopted by the Manchester Corporation In all cases of suspected aflutter ,tirin they armeslei to the cow, which was the only safe appeal. Other- wise It was really no disgrace to a farmer to be fined for alleged adulteration. This nwter would never be satisfactorily settled until the milk was collected in factories, cooled ormerlv. tested, and paid for according to quality, and gull on the butter fat teit. It was also necessity that the milk should he pasteurized and made f-ee from germs. Foreign zompetitori were doing these things and 83 must the English producers. (Applause) se discussion fnlliwl. Mr Mather a eked whether the Cheshire AS4lilig- tion confined itself strictly te Chsshire. He took it. that in that meeting of farmers there would be a number of Lancas'aire men. Mr Sadler state I that the Association had mem- bers from adjoining counties and any milk pre- ducats in the Warrington district were free to join the Cheshire Associatien. They had now over 800 members. (Hear, beer) Mr. Baxter. C.C., said there were mernbirs of the Aasociation in Dsrbyehire. Mr. Mather said he was afraid they would loqs the advantage of Mr. Banner's handsome offer if they joined the Cheshire Aaenciation. Mr. Ditchfield said he believed there would he great difficulty in forming an independent society for the Warrington district as the expenses would be much greater. The subscription to be Cheseire 1 Association was only 5s a veer. 1 A resolution was unanimously passed to join the Cheshire Milk Prolucers' Associa .ioa, with a e ee- naittee at Warrington to manage the work of the district.

div.head: LIBERALISM IN RUNCORN. -- Sir J. T. Brunner, M.P., at the Liberal Club.
div.p: LIBERALISM IN RUNCORN. -- Sir J. T. Brunner, M.P., at the Liberal Club.

Mr. S. Taylor presided at the Liberal Club lecture last Tuesday. when tna lecturer we Sir J. T. Brunner, Bart, M.P. Considering the inclemency of the weather the attendance was very large. Mr. Taylor having referred to the pleasure occupying the chair gave him, spoke of the high esteem Runcorn had for Sir John, even his political opponents, in their heart of hearts, had a good feeling towards him. (Hear, heir) Referring to tho growth of enthusiasm amongst Rencorn Liberals, Mr Taylor pointed out that since the lass election over 120 new members had been enrolled on the books of the Club, and some 35 boniest, papers, and periodicals were contributed to it. (Eear, hear) Though that spoke for itself, what was most pleasing, was the energy, good feeling, sad determination whica actuated their members. (Hear, hear.) During the last election he found that he must have said something that was not very acceptable to the Tory Party, for he had received from one of their Tory opponents an annoy- , mous letter, couched in ungentlemanly and cowardly terms. (Laughter.) He Was, he thought, coo well- known to Runcorn plople to take any heed of it, and only mentioned it because he thought of having it framed and presented to the Liberal Club. (Hear, hear and aughter ) In conclusion Mr. Taylor mooted the question of the. formation of a Liberal 200 for Runcorn. Sir John Brunner, who was received with loud ap- plauee, said be WAN extremely pleased to hear that the club was prospering. Since the election throughout the whole division there seemed to be a desire to make up for lost time,and that such a spirit had shown itself ' within the walls of that club was to him no matter of surprise. They should never foreet there WAS a great deal of difference bet seen a Liberal and a Tory. Doer% let anyone persuade them that it was a solid fact that party diffsrenc ta were disappearing in England. (Hear, hear.) It was far from true. When the time came aed he was returned to Parliament the Tory voted steadily in favour of class privileges—in favour of the people who did not work, and against the people who had to work for their living. (Shame.) It was always the same, therefore never be persuaded that a Tory was as good as a Liberal. (Hear. hear.) It wag their duty to help the Liberal Party, make sure that Liberal polities, and Liberal riolticiatis, guided not only he Government of their country—their two is:aeds —but of the whole Em- pire at large- (Hear, hear.) Dealing with the formation of a " 200 "for Runc4rn Sir .flian considered it ought to be a Liberal " 300" for Runcorn, with 30 eantains. (Hear, hear). Still he thouht it was a matter woicti could be postponed for a little time. He was not going to talk geueral politics to them, but thought he would interest them if he talked a little about gold. Sir John then sketched the Watery of gold-getting and ont-smt, and its effect upon trade and commerce. sho sine how birnettalism had died,and the disastrous effects that free , silver would have, and did have, in an far as the Latin Union was concerned, upon the commerce of the world. He also ably illustrated how the gold standard affected is some degree the conditions of the working people. When gold was pleetiful, commodities were dear ; and when gold wee scarce commodities were cheap. It any- thiog, the latter stage was the best for !the workitscrnan —the man with the fixed wage. The profusion of gold raised prices and stimulated busiress in so far as the gold owners required commodities, but when the price of bread Was tip, the man with the fixed wage,was, if anything, the worse off. Se warned them that gold was a teriible demoraliser, and he deplored the growth of the deeire for its increaeed pro- duction. It Was demoralising not only the social life of England, but the whole political life of the empire. He aelsod them in their p eitical work to try and redeem their country from this demoralising eff,ctond try and bring about a return of that old faith and g..odnees such as they had in days gone by. (Hear, hear). The lecture was listened to with marked attention. At it. cotrausion Mr A R Namara proposed, and Mr J M F s,cirLieci, a vote of thanks to Sir J fleunner. A vote of thanks to the Coairmau concluded the meeting,

THE °REED CHARITY.
This charity has been distributed to about 150 recipienteat Weston. The amount dispersed was rather less than last year in cousequen2e of a 80026- what small income. BARNWOBTEE GRAMBIAR. SCHOOL.

The va-ri—o-ne—local bodies woo hold tne right to elect representatives for the Farnworth Grammar School, have just made the following selections The Corporation ot Widnes, Mr F II Gossage and Mr Banana Carey the Justices, Mr Holbrook Gaekell, jun. and Major Lewis; the School Board, Mr T Sut- ton Timis and Major Wareing.
THE PROPOSED WARRINGTON AND NOaTHWICII LIGHT RAILWAY.

At the meeting of the Stocitton 'Heath Parochial Committee held last evening, a resolution was un- animously passed on the proposition of Mr. Clarke requesting the Runcorn Rural District Council to oppose the proposed Warrington and Northwich Light Railway scheme at the forthcoming in- quiry at, Warrington. . _

OAKLAND-STREET P.S.E. WinNES, After an interval of a month this series of deservedly popular concerts was resumed on Satur- day, when a capital varied programme was sub- mitted. The Rev U Barraclough presided over a very large audience. NELSON-STREET BAND OF HOPE, RimmtN. Tee opening meeting of this society was held in the schoolroom, Nelson-street, on Monday evening. The proceedings took the form of a lecture on "Temperance,' illustrated with a number of liede- light views, by Hr. A. Jones, superintendent of the mission. Short intervals were filled up with recita- tions by the Misses Greet and hughes and Master henry hales, and a dialogue by Messrs. G. Gatley, J. div.head: RUNCORN DURING THE LAST 100 YEARS.
div.p: RUNCORN DURING THE LAST 100 YEARS.

[BY 1111. W. iIA.NDLkY, J.P.] It might be appropriate to briefly refer to the progress ef Runcorn during Lae last 100 years A century ago the Census Act was passed, and the first census was taken in the early part of 1801. Every decade since that period the custom has been continued. Therefore starting 100 years ago was on perfectly safe ground 63 far as known population and other particulars respect- ing Runcorn were concerued. 'Eno place had only then begun to emerge from the state of a small village. Seventeen years before that the Bridgewater Dock and the ldcks leading dawn to the river were opened, and the effect of this upon the town has been most marked. Runcorn had been an important place in pre-Norman days but sank iato insignificance after the Norman Conquest. It seemed to nave remained ire that state for some three or four hundred years. Then it again raised its head and become a very important port in the year 1481 in the reign of Edward IV. At the time it excited the jealausy of Chester so mucn that Edward was induced to pass an ordinance or char- ter, and Chester succeeded in getting a document passed which ,prevented any vessel. sailing direct to Runcorn without first going up the Dee to Chester and recharter- ing. That would tend to reauce Runcorn to a very low level. In 1801 Runcorn consisted of 228 houses oialy,and its population was 1379-716 being males and 663 females, This population was an abnormally large oae for the number of houses. Taese tig,ures strike one that there must be some extraordinary reason for it, and it ' was possibly due to the fact that in that year the Old Quay Canal was being made. Up to that time, from 1720, :he Mersey and Jr well navigation proceeded out into the river estuary at Bank Quay, Warrington. In the year 1800 the Old Quay Canal was commenced, extending the' navigation to Runcorn, and completed in 1803. Runcorn by a document dated 1798, which was the year in which was obtained the Act or order for the construction of the Old Quay Canal, had a rateable value of £2463. Toe situation of the buildings indicated very largely tee occupation of the people. There were old houses at Top Lecks,in the neighbourhood of the Bridge- water Canal, Peaningten's Old Row, near the Old Quay Canal, and also some on Mill Brow in the neighbourhood of the quarries waicti were then working, and several down Halton-road and the Staabills. Agriculture was very largely carried on, so far as buildings indicated at Higher Runcorn, and along what was known as High'. Street. There were also a few cottages in Church- street. One of the last buildings of the old type stood on the site now occupied by the Salvation Army. One was still standing in Mount Pleasant and several sill in Canal-street. Canal traffic was mostly the trade of Runcera at that time. Tee canal had been opened SOME) seventeen years, and on the Bridgewater Canal there were 41 vessels or flats, and two special boats for the conveyance of passengers and luggage. They had an average tonnage of 50 tons each. Tile old dome was the only one they then possessed. The dock was put there for the Staffordshire trade, an industry which they retained to-day, the other business was through traffic between Liverpoel and Manchester, and simply passed through the locks at Ruacorn. The Old Quay Navigation, which was at that time known as the Mersey and Imola had 35 vessels,two of which plied between Liverpool arse Warsington, and 33 between Liverpool and Manchester. A very interesting document, printed in 1800, gave the names of every vessel and their Captains, ors both the ' Bridgewater, and Mersey and Ir well Nsyigetions. It is remarkable to find that the names to day connected with tne water traffic are the seine as those in charge of those very fiats, proving that the watermen, altho agh tee traffic was through, lived in the good old town of RUOC9ra. Several old fashioned craft remained if not the actual timbers it might be the frames of which the stock, lock and barrel had been repaired and renewed from time to time. The local government of • decade or two began in 1830, for in that year Runcorn plucked up its courage to build the old ['owe Hall. The first meet- mu in it was held on July 22nd, 1831. The Select Vestry, which had been in existence for soma time and which had brought the town into being, was the governing authority. la 1832 the first real attempt at local govern- ment was made by the establishment of a Board of Health, which was approved by the Lords in Council, Runcorn appeared to have been afflicted by a dire visitation of cholera and the duties of the Board were to abate that fell disease Two sad memories of this visitation are recorded on several inscriptions in our Parise Cherch grave yard as follows. " Sacred to the memory of John Dunn, Surgeon, who departed this life august 26ta, 1832. aged 28 years. His amiable and obliging manners endeared him to all who knew him, his 'arsenous exertions were kind St indefatigable to the sufferings of others during' the rage of cholera when he fell a victim to that disease. " Beneath this stone are deposited the remains of Jane the beloved and affectionate wife of the Rev J Walsh, who died of cholera, September 2 ed, 1832,a:zed 36 years and 10 months. Here also lie the ashes of Joseph her infant son, who died two days after of the same disease, aged 14 months." Dr Jahn Dunn and the Rev J Walsh were two of the most active members of the Board of Health one paying the penalty of lois devotion with his life and the other in tne loss of his wife and child They were succeeded by the surveyors of highways, and the inspectors of lighting and watching, wha held sway until the Improvement Commisleners were formed ia the early part of 1852. Then began the real local government of the town: There were in 1851, 1,710 in- habited houses, 108 uninhabited, and 15 in course of erection. The population had risen from 1379 to 8,688, composed of 4332 males, and 4356 females, including 220 to be found on canal barges. The rateable value of tile town had risen from £2,473 in 1800 to £22,710. Ii 1851 Runcorn consisted ef 65 streets,undrained and unpaved, and altogether very d fferent from its present state. In Halton Ward there were tii.!.ven streets, and sines than twelve have been added. Mersey Ward to seistea of 15 streets, and a similar number has eosin sine 3 made. In the Central Ward there were 30 streets one only having been added. Briigewater Ward was practically new, only containing the street known as the English Cresent and Welsh Row. Since that time this tees been increased 27. There were tbree in Newtown Ward, and sevea hi Heath Ward, and 15 have been respectively ad led to each. A total of 84 new streets have been made since the formatiou of the Runcorn Improvement Comaaissioners, toe number of streets excluding courts and passages now hAnv, 149 In 1852 the number of assessments was 1867, and on the previous Saturday that number had increassd to 4372. The rateable value has grown from £22,710 to £56,474, and the value of the works has gone fr om £7,906 to £14,550. It has substantially doubled itself in the 50 years. the 1901 census has not been taken yet, and one would not like to venture any definite opinion as to the population, but mu tiplying the number of inhabited houses by five invariably gives an approximate population. and it would very likely be fou ad that the Deputation of Run- corn would not number more that' 19.000. The popula- tion in 1891 wee 20,050, largely augmented by the work- men on tire Ship Caual, aria the taouses, which were practically all occeoted, were 3.831. The ratable value ' was in 1891, £60,876 toe ta.vu nss not yet recovered all that it lost with the slump in the chemical trade, and the closing of the works on the Ship Canal. Still there is very great hope in looking forward to the future

[By a Correspondent].

The question mooted at the Runcorn Liberal Ciub regarding the formation of a Liberal 300 is one of exc.-30411u promise..Titne has been when those who shJuld have figured as Liberal leaders Lave struggled strenuously to keep party politics out of local matt.rs. The last election had, as one of its immediate effects, the result of encouraging the Conservatives of the district ; and since, on more than one occasion, they have given evidence that they glory in a rising strength. This has been in a measure humiliating to the friends of Liberalism, but the steps that shall reinstate them in their past ascendency are at length being taken. The Liberal- ism of the locality, lik3 the Liberalism of the empire, has as it were passed through the" ordeal by tire," and the time is not far distant, when once more men shall raise their heads under its glorious banner of freedom and reform.

Proud Runcorn, and prouder Runcornians, will blush with shame co hear that one of its truest and best of frieuds, Mr S raylor, has been the recipient of an ungentlemanly and cowardly worded anony- mous epistle. Surely, the best ot us may differ in opinion without the use of what one of my own antagonists described " Liberal language,"though that was but the blunt straightforward English word "Liar," used unler strung prorwation, And methinks, to use such a word to the compiler of ' that dastardly epistle would be measurably justifi- able. Mr Taylor's idea to have it framed aud hung up in the Liberal Club is a good one, and would stimulate many to vindicate Li character by giving a ctlaracteristic awl emphatic denial to the whole. Runcorn Liberal:: know Mr Taylor, and can appre- ciate him, so to.) Clll the majority of his towns- people, but the one flaw in our return for all his generosity is that one Runcornian could be so mean as to "write what is wrote."

Sir John Brunner as a p Aitician wo know, and as such the Northwich Division has put faith in him for more than 15 years. At Runcorn Liberal Club, on Tuesday last, he figured —as a politician still—but not as a political politician, if the phrase be allowed. His teaching was against the demora- lising influence of gold,' and twe tendency of the times to lose i:ight of everything in the one desire to increase the "gilt, commodity." He prayed for a return to the "old faith and goodness of bygone days," when principle was honoured and " a good name was something more than gold." Lie showed the jugglery of the sharematlcet ; burst the bubble
,of bimetalism; and illustrated how the warkag. man of fixed wages was no IVJI:81: off the more gJil was procurable. No comes the question one A my own: " Was the War worth i?"

The Halton Parish Council, acting as a Parochial Committee, have been considering the question of sewerage, but their deliberations have not yet coma to any practical issue. The scheme most favoured by them was similar to the proposal for the sewer. ing of Daresbury, by means of filtration beds, a draft of which was submitted for their considera. Lion by the Clerk. HaLon, however, decided to wait until Darasbury had hid its scheme approved and in operation, preferring to be guided by practical results, rather than by theories. _lean. while things go on as they were.

The weather this week has been phenamenal aud the district has experienced a plunge from ideal summer, into the heart of winter, then after two days of severe frost and snow, the balmy days of spring prevail. Truly the weather is typically English and none but the phlegmatic Saxon can, pernaps, properly appreciate it. The frost whilst it lasted did little to impede business upon the local waterways—the Ship Canal and Bridgewater canal, but the poor of the town suffered greatly from the "nip." " The poor we have always with us." but that we think of them only when practical coai. passion is too late is often our self reproach.
