div.head: "THE UNTRODDEN PATH OF THE FUTURE."
div.p: "THE UNTRODDEN PATH OF THE FUTURE."

The above was the subject of the R3V A Wells' (super. intendent of the Runcorn Wesleyan Circuit) sermon, de. Livered espeeially ta young mea and maidens at St. Paul's Church, Runcorn, last Sunday night. The con. gregation was large and atteutiva. Taking for his text " For ye have not passed this way heretofore," Joshua iii. 4., he dwelt on toe similarity between the membern of that congregation and the children of Israel. They were on the verge of a New Year—a new century. Be- hind them was the past, before lay the "untrodden path of the future." What trials, troubles, temptations be- et their way they knew not, or what joys, what happi. fames teey would be comforted by they could not tell. The revelation of their path was in the light of the Lord Jesus Christ, that they did know. They would not have to tread that path companionless, and that was a point strongly emphasized by the preaaier: The choice of companion lay with them. - Whom to avoid they knew. But it was a point upon which he could not speak too strongly. Let them all seek those e'6nzpanions who exercised a lifting, holy influence upon them, and shun the world-loving, pleasure seeking, frivolous ones who rather tended to degrade. Youth was the season for cultivating habits. Let them see to it that no bad habits that enthralled aid fettered were the fruits of their youth. They knew it was passible for the criminal to evade the laws of man, but it was not so with toe eternal laws of God. They would be present who:ever they were and would have power and influence over them. There was no doubt about it, they were all mar- velously affected by their constitutions, but God tLad given them all a will of their own and would hold th‘na responsible for the control of those constitutions,through the use they made of their will power. Raving sketched the dangers of their path, he referred to the danger of the times in which they lived. Tne tendency of atheiiin was very very prevalent. That however was attributable to the conduct of the churches theuasiiices In the past. The " dritroddeu path of ccie future" was daily opening before them, ,ad he advised them all to get light. Get light from good books, good music, good people ; get light from anywhere and everywhere; but whatever they did be sure and get light from the Lard Jesus Christ, for it was Be and Be alone who would give them that white light which said " All right," and gave them a clear run Into Heaven.—At the close of the service the Anal's' Covenant Service took place, being conducted by the Rev A Wells, who was assisted by his colleague, the Rey J B Foster. The attendance was one of the largest ever known in the history of St. Paul's ; and, the whole Ser- vice was of a most divine character,and a time of special blessing. The offertory, which is devoted to the poor, amounted to £6 35 61.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
ALLEGED THEFT OF A POSTAL ORDER BY A
WARRINGTON POSTMAN.

James Francis Gartlaad, postman, 77, F lx-strect,was I charged at the Warrington Police Coutt on Monday with stealing on November 20th a letter containing a postal order of the value of 2s, the property of the Postmaster General. Mr Browne represented the defendant.—Mr James Alexandra Kirby, a clerk at the General Post I Office, London, prosecuted and asked that the defendant alight be remanded. On Saturday he had an interview with defendant at the Warrington Post Office. In the course of the interview be asked him to show him the contents of his pockets. He at first refused, but eventu- ally did so. He took from the pocket of the uniform coat he was wearing, a letter addressed by himself to a Erns of bookmakers in London. In the envelope were three postal orders atti a communication. The postal orders were issued at Sankey-green, and were payable to the bookmakers. For one of the orders be (witness) had had an application in connection with a complaint that a letter was missing. He asked defendant where he had obtained the postal orders. He said in the first instance they had been purchased by a girl who lived next door tohltn, and afterwards that he had purchased the parti- cular order mentioned. Defendant was a temporary auxiliary postman, and had been so employed from October 22nd, 1899. Mr. Browne did not object to the remand. He said the matter was an important one, not only to the Post Office but to the public. His client said he bought the order.—A remand for a week was granted

Swift were charged with trespassing on land in the posssession and occupation of Willians Bond, at Haydoak, in search of game on the 22nd of December. Neither of the defendants appeared, but on the application of Mr H 3 Longton, who appeared for the prosecution, the case was beard in their absence.—Mr Longton stated that at 10.3) on the morning in question a gamekeeper saw the two men trespassing on the laud. When he first discovered them. Swift was carrying a gun, but when the defendants became aware of his presence. Swift handed the gun to Mawson The keeper asked them for their names and addresses, and Mawson, who would not allow Swift to say anything, gave wrong names and addresses for both of them. When Swift attempted to speak. Mawson threatened him with his fist. It transpired that Mawson bad a licence to carry a gun, but Swift had not. The keeper did not see the defendants shoot at anything, but they were 300 yards sway from the foot- path. so they were evidently in search of game.—William Middleton, the gamekeeper in question, gave evidence bear- ing out the statement. When brought before the head keeper, the men made a lot of misrepresentations.—Mawson. who had been before the magistrates 13 times for similar offences was fined 403 and costs, and Swift, who had made Only one previous appearance, was fined ifs and costs. HAWKING WITHGUT A LICENCE,—John Swift was summoned for hawking without having a licence at Haydock on December 22nd.—Mr Farmer. the local Inland Revenue officer, stated that the defendant was In charge of a cart laden with hardware goods and ene or two cans of lamp-oil. He went from house to house endeavouring to sell his goods, and a woman living in Penny-lane bought some oil and a lamp from him. " Swift Brothers, licensed hawkers " was painted on he side of the vehicle. When asked for his licence, defendant said he had not got one but had applied for one. Ultimately it was ascertained that defendant's brother had a licence and defendant had been trading under it. A hawker's licence could only be used in the absence of the master by the servant. The brothers had dissolved partnership.—A fine of 108 and costs was inflicted.

_ At the Warrington Police Court on Tuesday, before Alderman Sutton and other magistrates, Aanie Clarke, who resides in Manchester-road, was charged on a warrant with obtaining the sism of 2; 6d by meana of false pretences from the Soldiers' and Sailors' Families' Asseciation, on December 7th —Mr Browne prosecuted on behalf of the Association and stated that the prisoner's son went out to the front with the South Lancashire Regiment. Arplication was made to the Association through the Beanr for relief and the woman was allowed 2s 6d weekly in February. In September prisoner informed certain persons that her son had been invalided home and was in Ne'iey hospital. The money continued to be paid to her, but in October. suspicions were aroused in consequence of it being heard that the prisoner's son had COMA home from the war. Mrs Dakin. the local bon seeretary, went to the prisoner and interrogated her about the matter, but she said her son was still at Netley. It subsequently turned out that the son was sitting in the hones at the time of Mrs Dakin'svisit. Eventually it was ascertained 'through the police, that the man had never been near Netfey'at all, but had been at home. MtPetiVe Meac-..ck visited the house on December Bth, and after some hesitation

Nis Clarke said her on was at home. Ile arrived at Warrington in Sapteinher..—The Chief Constable said a great deal of this sort of thing was going on in the town and neighbourhood and charitable institutions were euffering very considerably. Prisoner had t ^en bsfore the coult previously, for theft. The Bench imposed a penalty of 40s and costs (23 in all), with the option of 3 month's imprisonment.

SLEEPING OuT.—lfdvrard Hindley was charged with sleep- ing on the premises of Monks. Hall and Co.. Liverpoo'-road, without visihr means of subsistence, at midnight.—Samuel Mold, a watchman, stated that he was going round the works and found the prisoner in an ashhole asleep.—P.C. Orford, was charged with having been drunk in charge of a horse and vehicle. in Winwick-mad on December 21st, and with causing an obstraction in Bridge-street by leaving a horse and cart there on the same date.—P.C. (20) Cooper said the defendant's horse and cart were in front of the Lower Seven Stars Inn for three-quarters of an hour. Defendant was in the house. When he came out he was capable of tak- ing charge of the horse and cart, but was told he would be reported for causing an obstruction.—P,C, Lewis corrobor- ated—P.C. Hurst said he was on duty In WinwiCk-road on the evening of the same day, and saw defendant driving at the rate 'of about twelve miles an hour. He was shouting at the top of his voice. Witness called to him to stop, but he won'd not, He followed him to Warburton-street, and there saw that he was under the influence of drink.—P.C. Monks Corroborated, and defendant, was fined 10s. for the obstruc- tion and 10s. and costs for the other offence. £1 Bs. in all. WaDNPSDA.Y.—Before Mr. Birchall (in the chair), aldermen Sutton and Heaton.

STakNOE CONDITCT.—Harry Bolton Furness. a young man. Was charged with assaulting Ralph Long,manager for Messrs Furness and Company. Haydock-street, at two o'clock the previous afterneon.—The evidence of the complainant was to the effect that he was counting cash in the office when the prisoner came into the shop and a conversation ensued between Furness and his sister. Witness took no notice of this, and the prisoner entered the office. He said he would take the money if he wanted and witness told him he had better go out. That seemed to make prisoner a little excited and he seized him (witness) by the throat and threw him over the office chair, On regaining his position he held the prisoner until he got to the office door. When they were entering the shop prisoner saw a knife on a cheese and in his passion seized it. Witness told him to drop the knife and he would tllk to him and prisenerlimmediately became calmer. Whilst the scuffle was going on Mrs Long telephoaed to the Police Station for assistance and a sergeant came.—The.Bench imposed a fine of 5s and costs (El Cs 6cl In all.)

Prineesk-street- Runcorn, for being drunk in High-street, on the 26th Decem- ber, was fined ss.—George Millington. for being drank and' disorderly in High-street at 11.30 on Saturday night, was fined 54 and 6s coats.—lt appeared thatlthe defendant in this case committed a nuisance on the premises of Mr. Coventry, tailor; upon that gentleman coming out to remonstrate with him Millington threatened him with violence. OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.' --- Wycliffe P. 5.15. Society. There was an improved attendance at the meeting of this society on Sunday afternoon. Mr George Wallington occupied the chair and at the outset of his address he wished his hearers a "Happy New Year." He hoped that the P.S.A. Society would continue to prosper and that they might have good trade in Warrington. There was no doubt that many people in the town were begin- ding to feel the pinch of bad trade. In referring to the war in South Africa, he said he was delighted to see that there was a disposition on the part of some of our leading men to bring the conflict to a close. He was glad to see that Lord Kitchener was able to acknowledge the bravery of the enemy and it was to be hoped that his efforts towards bringing about a peace- able settlement would meet with success. The Boers had proved themselves brave men and it was for us to see that under British rule they were dealt with as free men, and then he thought there would be an honourable and lasting peace between the Dutch and British in South Africa, It was absurd for people to talk about the British Empire being broken up in consequence of the war in South Africa. England had gone through more than that in the past, and did they think that the Em- pire was going to fall to pieces because of 250.000 Dutch in South Afriea?—The address for the afternoon was de- livered by Mr .1 A Yonge, M.A. (principal of the Nor- thern Congregational School. SilcoateS, Wakefield). In an interesting way he drew some useful lessons from the poem of Thomas Parnell entitled "The Hermit." Mr Arthur Griffiths very efficiently sang two solos, entitled, "My hope is in the everlasting" and "The promised land."

div.head: DEATH OF MRS. SYLVANUS REYNOLDS.
div.p: DEATH OF MRS. SYLVANUS REYNOLDS.

Much regret was occasioned in Warrington on Tues- day morning, on the reception of the news that Mrs. Sylvanus Rovnolds, widow of the late Captain Reynolds, who formerly lived at Ridden-court, Latchford, had passed away at her residence, Wistaston Hall, near Crewe, on Monday evening. Tho deceased lady was well-known in Warrington and district and had gained the respect of a large circle of friends. It will be remem bered that the late Captain Rey nolds met with a severe accident while shooting on the 12th November, 1827 and died a few hours afterwards. His widow and family continued to live at Ridden-court for Some time after- wards, but they eventually removed to Whatcroft Hall, near Northwich, where, as in Warrington and district, they soon made a large circle of friends, and were deeply and deservedly respected. A comparatively short time ago Mrs. Reynolds took up her residence at Wistas- ton Hall, near Crewe,where she died on Monday evening The news created no little surprise, as it was not generally known she was ill. She was the mother of a large family. Two of her sons are now at the front, namely Captain Guy Reynolds and Captain S Reynolds, and each has many times greatly distinguished himself in the field. Mrs Reynolds, like her husband, took a great interest in politics, and was a very ardent politician on the Con- servative side. It was, however, in the Primrose League she took the most active interest, having for many years acted as Ruling Councillor of the Warrington Habitation of the League; in fact she held that position up to the time of her death. No Conservative ball in Warrington was regarded as complete without her presence, and she never missed a function of the kind when she lived at Latchford. The cause of death was failure of the heart's action.

div.head: Runcorn. Still Winning.
div.p: Runcorn. Still Winning.

To the chagrin of their supporters, the Horn Ate of Rochdale are still carrying-on in the same old unbu3i- nesslike way and losing matches. Each week during the past month have the epectators hoped to see a change in the team's form, but without result. There has been a slight improvement certainly,but the forwards still pack badly, and the backs show little or no cohesion. Run- corn were the visitors to the Athletic Grounds on Saturday, and they took a strong team. The Hornets were minus Blincow at centre, whose place was filled by Roebuck, frnm the •I A" team. Allen reappeared at half-back, with Harrill for his partner. The auburn-haired youth from Stock- port bad his arm hurt at Leigh, and be has been resting since. The visitors started with a deal more sprit than the Hornets. They went off with a rush which promigad to carry them over the line at once, but Rigg pulled them up just in time. Scrummaging followed in the vicinity of the Hornets' posts, and the defenders had to be very slippery indeed to checkmate the efforts of Jolley and D tvid Jones, They sacceoded in doing this,, and after Allen had changed the venue to midfield some capital footwork wss seen on the part of the home forwards,led by Owens. Houghton enlightened the proceedings with a strong run along touch which might have proved productive if he had not been left severely alone and unsupported. The Hornets retaliated by a clever movement in which Berrill, Field, Roebuck, and Richardson all showed to advantage. When the wing player found his path blocked be centred nicely, but Houghton under the most trying circumstances made no mistake and saved the situation. A minute later the ball was again travelling amongst the home backs, and Wightman, with a clear course, unfortunately slipped and vat collared. Runcorn, just to make things more interes - ing, rushed to the other end, and Walker broke away from a scrummage and scored, Jolley's shot at goal being unsuccessful. Ensuing play fluctuated a great deal, first one line and then the other being in danger, but no additional points were recorded before half-time. For a short time afterwards Runcorn had only seven forwards owing to one player getting his arm damaged. The Hornets accordingly beat them in the packs and got the pper hand, maintaining the advantage right to the

div.head: NORTHERN UNION. LANCASHIRE SENIOR COMPETITION.
div.p: NORTHERN UNION. LANCASHIRE SENIOR COMPETITION.
Warrington Unsuccessful at Swinton.

The all-conquering Swinton team was at home to War- I rington on Saturday,and the" wirepullers " bad for the second time this season to bow the knee to the Blues. Neither side was quite at full strength, but representa- tive sides were mustered. Warrington were without I Fish, Morrison, Duckworth and Mereweather, and the homesters short of Hampson and Messer. Splendid weather favoured the fixture, and the prospect of a plucky fight from the Warringtonians caused the specta- tors to roll up in large numbers,and there would be quite 6,000 :mei out at the commencement of hostilities. Mr Ashton, of Werneth, was the referee,and the teams lined out as follows Swinton: Chorley, back; Lewis, J. Valentine, R. Valentine, and Wallwork, three-quarters ; Davies and Morgan, half-backs; Vigors. Tickle, Berry, Jones, Porn- fret, Harris, Preston, and Murphy, forwards. Warrington: Hallam, back; flockenhail, Isherwood, Dickenson and Harris, three-quarters; Burgess and R. Bate, half-backs; Taylor, Boardman, Eden, Scholtze, Fairhurst, Swift, Pemberton and Cunningharn,forwards. Taylor started against the sun for Warrington, and the elder Valentine was soon tackled near the line. Daves relieved slightly with a smart run, Harris also , being tackled near centre by Wallwork. Warrington I kept up an attack, the Swinton men being too well watched to get away. Isherwood made a bad knock-on and lost his side a lot of ground, but the Blues were soon sent back again. Their fielding of the ball was very inferior to that of the visitors and they could make very little headway. Hallam had a shot at goal from a 1 penaltY, but failed. Then Morgan cleverly beat , the Warrington halves and fed Lewis who sprinted to half-way before being stopped. Taylor punted loftily from touch, and the Warrington front I rank travelled down the field in a body and prevented any return. Tight work followed on the home line, where the visitors strove hard to break through. Bate and Burgess passed out rapidly, and the tbree-cparters quite beat the Swinton men, Harris being robbed of a certain try through Dickenson knocking forward. Hockenhall varied matters by a smart drop at goal, which was the correct thing under the circumstances,

but success was denied him. Then Dickenson intercept- ed a pass and kicked past Chorley, who had a most ex- citing race for the ball with Hockenhall. The Waning- ton man had a glorious chance, but the home back was quite as speedy, and managed to kick dead from under the cross-bar Swinton worked hard to score, but could rarely Cross the centre line, so determined and safe was the play of Warrington. Several passing movements went wrong at the critical moment, Lewis being once ' sent in touch at the corner. Another rush by the War- rington forwards gained a lot of ground, for Pemberton ' very cleverly knocked Chorley's feet from under him, as he was on the run. The two Valentines did some excellent work,and play was fairly even till the interval, before which Jones went off with a nasty gash on the head. Half-time, no score. The Swinton skipper re-started the game, Jones hav- ing re-appeared with a bandage round his bead. The Blues showed that they meant business at once and entered the Warringtora half. Davies got away from a pack, aod a round of passing by the three-quarters re- suited in Jim Valentine scoring a fine try at the corner in his best style. R Valentine failed at goal. Warring- ton warmed to their work and rushed the game to the opposite end. Lewis dashed away down touch, Isher- wood grassing him ,finely, and Warrington again attacked. Fairhurst got the ball at his toes and dribbled to the line where Wallwo.rk saved grandly. It was a very near thing. Warrington looked like equalising, when a free-kick dashed their hones to the ground, one of R Valentine's huge kicks altering the condition of things very materially. Warrington passed well, but Isherwood was at fault and Swinton attacked. Some of the home for- wards over-ran the ball and Isherwood smartly picking up made a grand run tut° the home quarter. passing to Harris who nearly got through the Swinton defence. Chorley came away with a clinking run and passed to R. valentine, who muffed a fine spening. Just after three-quarter time Swinton became irresistible, and brilliant passing 91w Lewis in easily at the corner, no goal resulting. Warrington rallied again and even play followed, Burgess dropping unsuccessfully at goal. The Swinton backs played finely at this stage, and another series of bewildering exchanges left young Valentine in possession and he dashed over near the posts, the goal- I kick again going wide. Jones and Dal Davies then retired, the latter having injured his ribs, and just on time Chorley made a terrific running drop which landed the enly goal of the match nearly half-way. Final : Swinton, 1 goal, 3 tries (11 points) ; Warrington, nil.

finish. The rest of the story is soon told. The Hornets pressed nearly all the time, and the players were pulled up just short of the coveted position on several occasions. Wightman, Richardson and Field suffering in this way. Runcorn made only two incursions into the Hornets' quarters, but Walker scored another try. He got hold after some kicking, and ran straight in. Some of his opponents were under the impression that he was off- side—that was the general view amongst the onlookers —and did not try to stop him. The position was an easy one, and Farmer added the goal points. Runcorn there- fore won by eight points to nothing.

div.head: Widnes v. Oldham.
div.p: Widnes v. Oldham.
Widnes, who played at home, found their rivals rather too strong for them—Oldham winning by six tries to a goal. Barrow v. St. Helena.
Barrow was the venue of this fixture, the outcome of which was a win for the local club by fourteen points to five.
Leigh V. Stockport.
Playing upon their own ground Leigh experienced no difficulty in winning by two goals and four tries to a try.
Millom v. Broughton Rangers.
At Millom, the Rangers won by two goals and two tries to two goals. The game was interesting all through.
YORKSHIRE SENIOR COMPETITION.
Bradford v. Manningham.

Fully 13,000 people witnessed this mi,tch at Manning- ham, which Bradford won by two goals and two tries to nil. Cooper kicked the goals and Dobson and Robert- son got the tries. Wakefield Trinity vl Castleford.
A drawn game of two goals and three tries each was the result of this match at Castleford, Ball, Wark, Smith, Greenan, Speed, Goodyer, Bennett and Townend were the scorers.
Hunslet V. Holbeck.
The old rivals met at Hunslet, and the home side having distinctly the best of it all through, ran out easy winners by three goals and three tries to a goal.
Coeds v".. Hull Kingston Rovers.

Jackson and Colman scored for tbe home fifteen in the second half of this encounter at Leeds, and as Varley improved upon the latter's try, the Revers were beaten by eight points to nil. Hull v. Batley. In the opening half at Batley the nome side scored two goals and a try, and eventually won by these points to a try—gained by Hull towards the close of the game. Huddersfield v. Halifax.
At Huddersfield the visiting team were rather unex- pectedly beaten, after a keen struggle by four tries to one.

Liversedge v. Bromley. A capital struggle took place between these clubs at Liversedge. In the end Liversedge won by a try to a goal. Brighouse v. Leeds Parish Church. The home selection scored a goal in the early portion of this game at Brighouse, and this gave them the victory by two points to nil.

div.head: LANCASHIRE "A" TEAMS COMPETITION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE "A" TEAMS COMPETITION.

Warrington v. Swinton* Warrington "A n succeeded in disposing of the Swinton second contingent on Saturday. The home team commenced, and Sw inton failed to return, but forted the play to Warring ton's quarters,and from a free kick a goal was registered for Swinton: Radcliffe equalized shortly after with a splendid kick. The play was very even, and each end was visited in turn, both teams playing a grand game. Half-time ;—Warrington, two points ; Swinton, two points. The second half saw Warrington pressing to a considerable extent, until a bout of passing transferred the play, but again War- rington pressed, and Swinton were forced to touch down. A moment later, Radcliffe added another goal to Warrington's score. This was followed by Radcliffe dropping a third goal. The play was always in favour of Warrington after this. Final :—Warrington, six points; Swinton,two.
LANCASHIRE JUNIOR LEAGUE.
Latchford Rangers v. Widnes White Star. - - - -

At Latchford. Latchford kicked off, and for some time play ruled even. Widnes then rushed down, Wheat scoring at the corner. A fine bit of play by the Wi dnes backs saw Wheat score again, the goalkeeper failing. Half-time :—Widnes White Star, six points ; Latchford Rangers, nil. During the second half the visitors had the best of matters and added a goal and a try, finally winning by eleven points to nil.

div.head: FRIENDLY MATCH.
div.p: FRIENDLY MATCH.

WERNETH v, FLETCHER RIISSELL'3.—This ordinary en- counter took place at Werneth on Saturday. Fletcher's placed a moderate team in the field, several of their players missing the connection, and the full complement of players was made up of enthusiasts who bad travelled with the team but who had given up the serious side of the game. Play was at once carried well into the visitors quarters, but the latter gradually worked the ball back, Brady putting in long kicks and tackling well. Allen put in a long run, and passed to Foster, who was pushed in- to touch near the quarter flag. The visitors next became aggressive, and after pressing for Borne time Brown made a good attempt to drop a goal, but amends were made shertly afterwards by Ashurst dropping a goal. Fisher intercepted a kick, and passed to Whitworth,who rounded several of his opponents and crossed the line, but Wood failed to add any points by the kick at goal. Balf•time score.—Werneth, one try (three points) ; Fletcher Russell's, one goal (two'points). During the last stage of the game the Warringtonians were aggres- sive nearly the whole of the time and only the resolute tackling of the home men prevented the score being aug- mented. Eventually Paden dropped a fine goal, and the visitors thus confirmed the result of the first meeting the final result being Fletcher Russell's, two goals (four points); Werneth, one try (three points.)

div.head: ASSOCIATION I-OOTBALL. LANCASHIRE LEAGUE. Earlestown v. Wigan United.
div.p: ASSOCIATION I-OOTBALL. LANCASHIRE LEAGUE. Earlestown v. Wigan United.

Played at EArleszown on Saturday. Houghton, late of Newton-le-Willows was down to play for Earlestown, but he failed to put in an appearance, and as a conse- quence the homesters had to take the field ,with ten men. Play had not been long in progress, however, when Lee turned out to complete the eleven, Wigan won the toss and Brown started against the hill in the presence of about 500 spectators. A nice passing movement between the whole of the home forwards was the means of trans- ferring play to the Wigan goal, and Bartley shot hard and true for Hodson who had to concede a corner. This I was well placed and rebounded off Mills to Bartley who I banged the ball into the net the custodian having no 1 possible chance of saving. Straight from the centre kick the hotnesters again swooped down on the 1 Wigan goal and the leather eventually came out to Brown who dribbled clean through the defence and defeated Hodson for the second time. At the interval Earlestown were leading by two goals to nil. The resumption again saw the homes tete take the offensive, and Leach was going well for goal when he was foully if within the twnlve yards line. Settle took the penalty kick and scored Earlestown's third goal. The Wigauers seemed to rouse themselves after this and from v bully in front of Chew the leather was rushed into the net. Just before the finish however Brown put on No 4 for the homesters who ran out easy winners by four goals to one.

div.head: WHEN YOU'VE YOU'VE A :COLD.

MEN WHO FAIL AT 40.
MR. JAMES MEASOM, of 22, Middle-street, Leicester, told a Midland Free Press reporter of a remarkable experience. He is employed

as a " fettler " in a wool factory, and a wife and family are dependent upon his earnings. At an age when strong men are in their prime —forty years—he gradually became sick and ailing. "A great weakness came on," he said; "I lost my appetite, and became so debilitated that I could hardly walk about; I fell away two or three stone in weight. The complaint seemed to affect my chest and my breath, and I had a bad cough. I was under one medical man for nine months, but the nature of my illness was never put on the certificates. My mother read so much about Dr. Williams' Pink Pills that she thought 'I should try them. I did, and began to feel better by the time I had finished a box and a half. I kept on, and took six boxes altogether. I had been laid up unable to work for nine months, but I went back to work after taking three boxes of Dr. Williams' Pink Pills, and I feel strong and well."
DISORDERS OF DIGESTION.
A Strong Man Made Helpless. ONE of the staff at the pumping station of • Birmingham's great waterworks at Aston, is Mr. Thomas Smith, whose home is at 404, Lichfield-road. He has been employed

there for a number of years as stoker, but eventually found his health and strength giving way. He fought hard against what appeared to him to be an unknown disease, consulting several medical men and taking medicine without deriving benefit. He con- tinued to suffer for nearly a couple of years until, as he remarked to a representative of the Aston Times, "I felt as if I should have to 'jack' up. I first commenced to suffer from Indigestion and Biliousness, while at the same time a yellowness like jaundice broke out almost over my entire body. I suffered excru- ciating headaches, while the biliousness was horrible. I could eat nothing at all in the shape of solid foods, but now nothing goes amiss, and I can eat anything." The answer to a question as to what cured him, was one full of unmistakeable meaning. "Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People; they proved a wonderful remedy in my. case. I read in the Birmingham Argus a case similar to mine, and I determined to try the pills, beginning with one pill after each meal. I soon began to feel a change, and, persevering, I was quickly able to go about my work with ease. The headaches vanished after a few doses, and the biliousness also passed away, while the skin gradually resumed its original appearance and I was completely cured."

div.head: AGE 25: Strength Restored.
div.p: AGE 25: Strength Restored.

PRIVATE TIMOTHY WALSH, No. 4293, on the reserve of the 6th Inniskilling Dragoons, was called up last January, and is now on active service in South Africa. About the end of last year a North British Advertiser reporter called at his home, x, St. Bernard's-place, Edinburgh, and learned the following "I am twenty-five years of age," said Mr. Walsh, "and was for some years in the 6th Dragoons. In February, /899, I had a very severe attack of Rheumatic Fever, and had to be taken to`a hospital. I was quite helpless, and had to be lifted out of and into ray bed

like a child. After the fever left me I was sent home, but the pains were,as bad as ever. I lost my appetite and could get no sleep. I could not move without the aid of crutches. One doctor called it Acute !Rheumatism, but did not seem to be able to do me any good. Then a neighbour, whose son is in the habit of taking Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People, recommended them, and, on his advice, I started taking the pills. I had taken only two boxes when I began to feel great benefit, and I have improved ever since. Very soon I was fit to resume work at •engineering, which is my trade." The fact that Mr. 'Walsh subsequently passed the Army doctors, on being examined for active service, is sufficient corroboration of the above facts.
CHEST TROUBLES THAT FOLLOWED INFLUENZA.

MR. JOHN WAIN is a collier, forty-four year of age, living at 5, Abbey-terrace, Bucknall Stoke-on-Trent. This is Mr. Wain's some- what remarkable story, told to a StaPrdshire Sentinel reporter. " The torturing ailment with which I suffered for a very long time was an acute attack of Bronchitis following Influenza. The complaint developed a nasty painful cough and choking tightness of the chest, which made it very difficult to get my breath, and exhausted me generally. I got so bad that as soon as I was out of bed I began to cough, becoming so bxhausted that I could not get toy wind, and had to sit down before I could dress myself. From bad I went to worse, and had to call in a doctor; but this did not give me the relief I hoped for. My society lodge (the Druids) sent me away, but there was no lasting good from the change."

div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY JANUARY 11 1901. OLD FOLKS TREAT. PROCEEDINGS IN PARR HALL.
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY JANUARY 11 1901. OLD FOLKS TREAT. PROCEEDINGS IN PARR HALL.

Parr Hall was one again the sceue on Thursday last week of the annual Old Ken's Dinner and Aged Women'a Tea. This yearly function which the old folks may rightly call their own, is looked forward to with considerable pleasure by nose whose went it is to I accept the hospitality of the committee. At noon o n Thursday about 30) men gathered round the festive beard and ttiev were waited upon by a number of local ladies and gentlemen. A smile lit up the rugged countenances of this gathering of, W arringtott veterans as they feasted and chatted together of old times in the "good old days" of long ago. A substantial meal of beef, pork, and mutton, potatoes and vegetables, land plum pudding, was thoroughly enjoyed by the 1290 guests present, the great majority of whom were over 60 years of age. The oldest guest present was Mr John Clayton, of Poulton, who is 87. During ithe dinner, selections were played on the organ, by Mr WS Woods, formerly organist at the Parish I Church, and a graphaphone entertainment was pro- vided by Mr Joseph Roberts, of Fearnhead. The members of the committee had the assistance of a number of ladies and gentlemen in attending to the wants of the guests. The officials were as follows :—Alderman Sutton (president), Counoillor Smethurst (vice-president), Messrs D Jones and P Caldwell (hon vice-presidents), Mr T A Sutton (hen secretary), Mr P Chritnea (hon treasurer), and Councillors A Jolley, John Sampson, W ' J Forshaw, and T Burton ; Messrs D eanshaw, G Pill- lug, H Toll. H Singleton, R Shackleton, J Nield, and ii Bunch. One or two of these gentlemen were unable to lbe present. There was, however, no lack of willing 1 workers, and all of them were assideous in their work. The Revs E C E Carleton, E R Tarbuck, and W Brace- camp were amongst the visitors present. Beer and Itobacco were distributed. At the conclusion of the dinner a short entertainment was provided. Alderman Sutton conducted the proceed- ings and in the course of a few introductory remarks he wished all present a happy New Year. Be hoped that this, the first year in the new century would be one of the happiest and most prosperods in their lives. (Hear, hear.) Everyone who had participated in the dinner had lived through more than half of the past cen- tury and they would have witnessed the many wonderful changes which had taken place. They would have witnessed the advancement in science and art and the extraordinary rapid progress in connection with oi le ondc rniriarc during that comparatively 'short period. Jot introduction of steam en,Aines and 11 steam power lea ' .abled us to travel to almost every Ipart of the w in a comparatively short time. The telephone enabled us to converse with our business or 'private friends in different parts of the kingdom almost asifreely as though we were in the same room together. By the telegraph, messages could be transmitted thou- sands of miles in a few seconds, and electric cars were fast converting our highways into railways and enabling us to travel on the roads at railway speed. The speaker proceeded to refer to the wonderful changes in the newspaper press, which kept them in constant touch with every part of the world for a half-penny,and also made mention of the improved postal facilities. None of them would be able to see the dawn of the next century, but he hoped they would all live to see some of the important changes which were certain to take place in the near future. He would not be sur- prised if some of them lived long enough to see the day when people would travel in the air at almost lightning speed. (Laughter.) During the past year death had re- moved from their midst some leading townsmen. lie , was sure they all regretted the death of Alderman J E ' Wright. (Hear, hear.) After paying a tribute to the memory of Alderman Wright the speaker expressed the wish that those present might attend similar gatherings in year:Me come. He concluded by proposing the toast of :"The Queen." The toast was drunk with musi3al honours, Mr. Fan- shaw leading the singing. Mr. BAILEY, one of the recipients of the treat, after- wards complied with a recitation. Mr. PETER CHRIMES submitted a brief statement of accounts. He said he was glad to be able to tell them that they were in a better position than in the previous year to the extent of £lO. (Hear, bear.) It was prob- able that there might be a slight falling off in the funds owing to the numerous appeals necessitated by the war. but notwithstanding this he believed they would be able to have a Lood balance at the bank after meeting all expenses. Mr. Wit,cox was encored for a humorous song, alter which Councillor SMETHURST briefly addressed the company• During the prsG 18 years nearly the whole of the mem- bers of the original committee had passed away. He believed that within the last sevea or eight years of the ' 40 members of the Warrington Town Council 22 of them were now out of that assembly. He proceeded to refer to the usefulness of the late Alderman Wright who was a valued member of the treat committee. Some selections were given on the graphaphone by Mr. Roberts, and at the close The Rev. E. C. E Museums proposed a vote of thanks to the officials and Committee of the Institution. The work they did was a very important one, and one that enlisted the sympathy of the whole town. He hoped they would not forget the absent members of the Com- mittee' and he proceeded to allude especially to the work which had been done in past years by Mr. Daniel Jones. (Applause). He trusted that very soon peace would be restored in South Africa and that those who had left Warrington for South Airier, and who had spent Christ mas teem would shortly return and receive that welcome they all desired to givethem. (Hear, hear). The Rev E R TARBUCIC seconded, and said he would have liked to see the old men and women sitting down together, but he supposed there was not a hall large enough in the town to accommodate them. lie was sure they were all extremely gratified at the excellent arrangements which existed for giving this annual treat. (Applause). Tne;vote on being put to the meeting was unani- mously passed. The Chairman responded end the pro- ceedings terminated with the singing of the National anthem. Tea was provided for about 500 women in the after- noon, and the proceeedings were again attended with success. Excellent arrangements had been made, and they were carried out without a hitch. After the repast, an entertainment was provided, to which the public were admitted. Alderman Sutton presided, and in addressing the guests of the evening, he expressed the hope that they might be present at similar gatherings for many years to come,and that the remaining years of their lives might ba attended with much hapoinesS. (Applause.) He must congratulate them upon their good looks. (Lauehtere He understood that the oldest lady present was 83 years of age, but it was a difficult matter, he facetiously observed, to ascertain the real age. (Laughter.) He regretted that at the beginning of the century, trade was so bad in the iron trade,and that many families were suffering in consequence of it. He hoped that the present depression' would shortly pass away and that the good wages of their husbands and sons would make them as comfortable as possible. He should be very glad indeed if the workingmen of this country would consider their interests more than they did. There were many of them who earned good wages and yet they never attempted to put aside anything for a rainy day. They were no better off at the end of a boom in trade than at the beginning and the result was that when there was a depression in trade they had to resort to the relieving officer or to friends in order to live at all. The speaker proceeded to refer to the fund.; of the institution and said that Mr Thomas Fletcher had headed the subscription list with £lO. (Applause). An entertainment was thee proceeded with. Mr William Kilduff was very successful in a character sketch entitled "An incident from South Africa," and as an encore he sung "Sweet Genevieve." Miss Agnes Rig- by contributed two songs entitled the " Kerry Dance," and "The old folks at home," and the Misses Dell gave a duet on the mandolines "Coralie•" The humour of the evening was supplied by Mr Matt Kilduff, whose charac- ter song, "The sour apple tree" was one of the most en- joyable pieces of the evening. The St Mary's Amateur Dramatic Society was very successful in the farce "The Siamese Twins," the characters being taken by the following :—Captain Vivid, Mr J R Knox; Dennis O'Gib, Simon Slow, (the twins) Mr A Bate and Mr H Rovlance ; Mr Firceps (A Virtuoso) Mr S Ryan; Marian (Ward of Mr Firceps) Miss A Kilduff; Sally (A Servant) Miss Cissie Burrows ; Stage Manager, Mr William Kilduff.

The proceedings terminated with the sinoing of the National Anthem. Mr W S Woods presided 's at the or- gan, and Mr Frank Booth was the accompanist on tha piano. On leaving, each guest was presented with an orange and a mince pie.
ANGLERS' ANNUAL MEETING.
A Successful Association,

In the Druids' Hall, Sankey-street, Warrington, on:Thursday last weak, the annual general meeting of the Warrington Anglers' Association was held.. Mr J Lyon Whittle presided, and he was accom- panied on the platform by Mr Peter Knight (secre- tary), Mr F J mson (assistant secretary), and Mr A Cook (treasarer). The Chairman, in opening the proceedings wished the members a "happy new year." Might it prove a prosperous one, and as anglers he trusted they might have full baskets (Hear, hear). _

div.head: ANNUAL REPORT.
div.p: THE ANNUAL REPORT.

Mr F J EMBO-N read the tenth annual report of the Association. In presenting the report, he said the committee congratulated the members upon the continued prosperity of the Association. At the end of 1899, they had a membership of 380. They had now reached a total of 446 members, including 32 members of the juvenile branch, an increase of 60. (Applause). They had 464 members enrolled on the books, of which number they had 18 who had riverreference G o w yt o at thsksioec arta ffo no Ai'red rnroi vt jactee wwaast fe or rs not subscribed anything and 13 partly paid. With wi na rtdheed to Mr Maynors, the Earl of Shrewsbury's agent, surrendering the fishery. A correspondence, how- ever, was taking place between the agent and the Association with a view to a reduction of rent, and should this be obtained,the committee might be die posed to continue the tenancy. The Association had been enabled to secure the exclusive right of fish- ing from Mr Hassell, of Bridge Trafford Hall,on the whole of his land fro.m Trafford Bridge to the point known as Shaker Bridge. The Lymm water, though it had fished somewhat better than the previous year, was not yet as satisfactory as they could de- sire, especially as, they stockea the water last winter with a considerable quantity of course fish. Visitors explain the lack of sport, first, because it seems naturally a late water, and secondly, to the numbar of pike that abound in it. The river Bollin, which was secured during 1899 had fished fairly well during the past year, and they bad . every reason to believe that I they had a bright future in store for them. In addition to the 700 large trout presented to them by their chairman during 1899, a further con- signment of about 300 was presented from the same source in the early part of 1900. And further, Mr Whittle had kindly hatched out and presented to them about 10,000 fario, Rainbow and Loch Leven ova, which had been transferred to the " newly-erected rearing pond at Heatley. (Applause.) These fish, they assumed would be of such a size, that they would be enabled to turn them into the main stream early in the ensuing year. Especial mention should also be made that Mr G S Smeeth, of Manchester, obtained about 1,000 fario ova and very kindly presented them to the Association. These were duly hatched out by Mr Whittle and would form part of the future stock. (Hear, hear.) Reference was made to the excellent services of Mr Edward Porter, an old member, as watcher for the Association who had also made himself familar with the more arduous duties of fish rearing. A small rearing pond on the Warburton estate had been provided under the direction of Mr John Newton, of Warburton, who de- served the thanks of the members for the interest he evinced in the affairs of the Association. A much better feeling now existed between them and the tenants on the different estates, and it was felt that the best interests of both parties were se- cure under the arrangements now made, It was expected that the fishing owned by Mr Heathcote, which extended on the very lowest portion of the Bollin on the Lymra side, would soon ba made over to them, and thus a continuoas length of about six miles would be secured on this popular river. Dealing with the Old Quay Canal, which had been a source of trouble and anxiety to .them, they might say that pumping operations which. wrought such destruction amongst the stock in 1899, had been permanently stopped, it and had become so promis- ingthat they had decided to restock the canalovith the earnest hope that this local and con- venient fishery might for the future escape further accident and be a source of sport and enjoyment in the future. The animal angling contests of the past year had been fairly successful, the number competing teaching a higher figure than in any previous year. The catches were not of a satisfactory character, the fish being, on the whole, small. All the prizes, which were of a valuable nature, were won however. The gold medal, which was a special prize with certain con- ditions, presented by the esteemed Chairman, and also a silver medal presented by Mr W H Pod.more, were competed for by the winners of prizes in the contests, and were won respectively by Mr T Robin- son and Mr W Birchall. The specimen fish contest had not been quite so successful as last year, the amount in prizes being .£7 7s as against .C 8 5s the previous year. On carefully going through the books, it was found that members had weighed in Association 97 fish of a total weight of 1201bs 2oz.s. sclrs.Twenty- two prize fish had been Cauglit in waters and 18 in foreign waters. The juvenile branch had been a distinct success. There had been a satisfactory increase of ten mem- bers and they 'had been able to offer in addition to the usual contest, prizes for speci- mens of four classes of fish, caught in home and foreign waters. The secretaries were sorry to have to record the deaths of the following members of the association during the past year :—Messrs J Welsby, W Bolton, J Standish, G Bennion and Charles Spencer, who was killed whilst on active service in South Africa in November. In conclusion the Committee claimed that during the past 3 ear the interests of the members had been well considered, and that every effort had been made to place the Association in the forefront of the fraternity. Mr. J. PODAEORR proposed the adoption of the report. Mr. WOOD seconded, and the report was adopted.

div.head: BALANCE SHEET.
div.p: THE BALANCE SHEET.

Mr COOK presented tno annual financial statement. The income for the year including a balance of £5 65 brought forward amounted to £l7B. After meeting all lexpenses there was a balance in hand of £8 2s 'ld. A considerable sum had been spent in providing a rearing pond. It was beautifully situated and the fish number- ing 10,000 were thriving. (Hear, hear.) Mr WOOD called attention to the expenses incurred in removing fish to the association wat!rs. He would be pleased to place his horse and fiat at the disposal of the committee free of charge for that purpose. (Hear. hear.) He proposed the adoption of the balance sheet. Mr Boscow seconded and the report was adopted. THE PRIM. 1 Mr KNIGHT gave particulars relating to the prize com- petitions. 97 memberf weighed in fish as speoimens, and the number of prizes given was 32.

RE•ELECTION OF OFFICERS. Mr ERNEST ERO3FIELD was re-elected president, Mr Peter Knight, secretary ; Mr F J Emsoa, assistant secretary ; Mr A Cook, treasurer ; and the following were appointed vice-presidents :—J L Whittle, L Green- ing, J L Tunstall, W S Haddock, A. Lister Kaye, E Milner, A C de Boinrille, Rev E B. Tarbuck, W Rams- bottom, W Chambers, W II Podmore, James Mottram, William Wood, William Brown, W A Proud, John Mawson,T Beswick, W Lever, William Taylor,B Hendry F J Bonnie, E Pickavauce, and T J Garnett. The meeting then terminated.

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS.
Despatch from Lord Kitchener.
Severe Fighting.
87 British Killed and Wounded.
35 Boers Left Dead on the Field.
The War Office on Thursday isolated the following from Lord Kitchener .
PRETOM, January 9.

On the night of the 7th the Boers made a simul- taneous and detenn7ned attack on all our posts at Belfast, Wonlerfontein, Nnoitgedacht, Wildfontein, and Pan. A dense fog prevailed, and taking advan- tage of the csver it afforded the Boers were able to creep up close to our position._

Heavy fire continued until 3.40 a.m., when Boers were driven off. One officer (Captain Fosbery) killed, and three officers wounded, 20 men killed, 59 wounded. 8041083 heavy, 21 dead being counted. A convey taiWg supplies to Gordon's Brigade north of Brugersport was attacked by Beyer's com- mando yesterday. The Boers were driven off, leav- ing eleven dead on the field; our casualties four men slightly wounded.
THE CAPE INVASION.
Large Defensive Operations.
CAPETOPIN, ThursdAy.
Our forces now occupy all the most important strategic positions, including Pickaneer's Woof and the Pignetberg district.

The Capetown Guard will be inspected on Satur- day. They wear badges similar to those adopted by the forces raised daring the Fenian scare. The men are armed with Martinis. It is expected that 5,000 will parade on Saturday.:

div.head: Interesting War Relic.
div.p: Interesting War Relic.

An interesting. war trophy is on view in the window of the Viliemarleigh Cafe. Sankey-street, in the shape of captured Boer flag.. Near it is the following eKpiana- tic.n :—" Presented to the Mayor, in recognition of the terest shown by the people of Warrington in the men at the front and their wives at home, by Private W. Makin, 3rd P.W.V., South Lancashire Regiment. Kruger's Siding, Orange River." The trophy, which is the object of much interest, was received in Warrington on the 7th instant.

div.head: 'KRUGER AND KHAKI?' -- Mr. F. Villiers Lectures at Earlestown,
div.p: 'KRUGER AND KHAKI?' -- Mr. F. Villiers Lectures at Earlestown,

On Wednesday evening the Viaduct Institute, Earlea- town was crowded on the occasion of a lecture by Mr lF Villiers, artist, entitled "Kruger and Khaki." Colonel Pilkingten should have presided, but being indisposed,ho Was unable to be present, and the position was filled by the Rev C E Dove. . .

The Chairman said that the gentleman who had kindly Consented to preside over that lecture, the member for the division, Colonel Pilkington, was indisposed, and- was unable to be present. Under the circum stances, he thought the most fitting chairman would have been their excellent President, but be declined, hence his (Mr Dove's) presence. He need Scarcely say that he was glad to be present. He partici- pated to some extent in their privileges, and he bad no desire to shirk the responsibility. He took the chair more readily because no speeches were required. He Would say just one word on the subject. They all felt whether they were pro-Boers or Britishers that they were greatly indebted to our dear fellows who were in South Africa and sincerely hoped that hostilities would soon cease, and that the men would soon return home. (Arplause.). The light was then turned down, and Mr Villiers proceeded with his lecture, which was nothing more nor less than a description of the war, as he saw it, from Megersfontein. to the capture of Crorje, accompanied by lime light views, At the outset he criticised the reproductions of snap shots said to have been taken during the progress of a battle. There bad, he said, never been so much fraud practised with the camera on the public, as during this campaign. Think of the snap shots they had seen, ostensiblv taken in the firing line Ho dwelt on the fact that the Government was able to transport such a vast army of soldiers six thousand miles by sea, and had peeved to the world that the British Empire was at one and that the wide branches of this great tree were not choked by Socialism but were growing in perfect freedom. He then pro- ceeded to give a simple account of the war, pall ing here and there to pay a tribute to the rnem)ry of fallen generals, and to the bravery of the British s-ldier. The pictures he produced were very good,and helped greatly to illustrate his descriptive account. He testified to the excellent way in which the private soldier was treated, both in regard to commiaaariat and in ambulance treat- ment. His concluding picture was a port-alt of 's The Queen," the audience singing the National Anthem.

The Special Com- mittee to have full power to assent to or dissent from the proposals of the said Company, in whole or in part, as may after consideratin -, appear to them advantageous to the interests of this district, and for that purpose they be hereby empowered to make such arrange- ments and to incur such expenditure as may be neces- sary for the protection of the inhabitants of the district. The Clerk rea3 a letter whichlie had received from Messrs Gillespie and Mason, Ltd., with respect to the width of the road along which the South Lancashire Tramways Company propose to construct a tramway leading from this district along Mill Lane to Warrington and his reply thereto stating that the Council will take steps to safeguard the interests of the public. The Clerk read a letter which he had received from the Sac retary to the Lancashire Electric Co., with respect to the supply of electricity in bulk. It was revolved that it be a recommendation to the Council to apply to the Board of Trade for a previsional order to autberise the Council to supply electricity for all public and private purposes within the District of Newton-in-Maksrfield. The Clerk read a letter which he had received from the General Manager of the Loudon and North- Western Railway in reply to the letter which he addressed to the Secretary of the Company on the 6th inst,upon the subject of the accnm- mndation at the Earlestown passenger station, stating that the matter is one which they have had fully under consideration, and that in all probability no great time wniald elapse to,fore the directors see their way to authorise an improvement of the•accemmndation. A lade • was read from Rev J Ryder. Vicar of St. Peter's Newton- le-Willows, inviting the members of the Council to a service at St. Peters Church on the 2nd January to mark the opening of the new century. At a further mentinr of the committee held on Mon- day afternoon, Mr Forwood. of Messrs F J Leslie and Company came before the Committee with respect to the requirements of the Couecil as to Southworth-road, and Mill-lane in connection with the proposed new line of tramways from the Town End Bridge at Newton along the Warrington highway through Winwick to Warring— ton sod agreed on behalf of the cnmpany to insert a clause in the proposed Bill meeting the requirements of the Council and agreeing to widen Town End Bridge tO27ft.in accordance with the requirements of tho County Council CEMETERY COMMITTEE. . .

Mr Simpson prnirsel the confirmation of the minu'es of the Cemetery Committee which had been named that dav with reference to the N-w Burials Act. It was deci- ded to write to the Local Government Board for a sug- dested table of fees, showing the maximum and minimum fees allowed. Mr Gilmour objected, an 4 said he did not think it was wise to introduce sulsid;ts of which the members had had no notice. The minutes were passed,

NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS. Rugby Football. [By " Ovalisti Fortune doe 3 not always follow the brave. There can be no doubt that Warrington were brave on S aturday and mad a very plucky fight against the all conquering Swinton" Lions" but Dame Fortune, was looking the other way when Warrington tried to cttch her smile. The visitors had hopes, born of determination and a delusive victory at Manningbam, that they might put a spoke in Swinton's wheel of SUCC"33, ant their temerity was properly punished. For half the gam, however, Warrington were the aggressive party and the possibility of a surprise was not very distant. Later on the finish and training of the Limo team became more apparent and the result was only what tin average individual expected-11 points to nil in 9winton's favour.

The only thing which does not redound to Warring- ton's credit is the fact that they were "nil ed " It looks 'asif a team has been hopelessly out ot it when the. winning side compiles a goal and three tries to nothing Now, Warrisraters were by no means hopelessly out of it' in fact they gave the BiLIPS nearly as tough a struggle as they endured at Wilderspool. Taking the game right through I think the losers were oftener attacking than the winners, though the methods of the two sides were I 1‘ very different. Warrington attacked with dogged per; sistence which deserved some reward, and the homes- tars attacked with combined brilliance which there was no resisting. liip to the interval almost all the attack- ing came from the visiting side, and there was some anxiety visible on the faces of the sp.ctstors. Warring- ton's lack of scoring power was evident to the close ob- server, nevertheless, for the backs entirely lacked the speed necessary to turn an opening t, the best, advan- tage. For instance,on one occasion the ball was punted past Chorley, the home full back, and roiled under the posts. Hockanhall and be had a level race for the •* object ball "and the Swintonian won, and not only won bllt gained a yard on his pursuer. A fast wing man would have got an easy try there, but Hockenhail was not speedy enough. Yet he is as fast as any mem- ber of the Warrington team as composed or. Saturday. , Man for man the home team were much the speedier, and it was speed more than cleverness that got the . poi ats.

The fact is indlsputable.that Warrington are not in the name class as Swinton, even though under enceptional circumstances they might defeat the Blues. Supposing Warrington to have been strong enough forward to have controlled the packs, then the team might have gained the verdict, but this would not have raised them to a level with the losers all the same. Swinton are wonder- fully strong in all departments and even forward they were better than Warrington,. while the backs were as much superior as those of Waies are over the chosen of England. La all probability Warrington will have to play Swinton in the final of the South West Lancashire cup, and the team will have scarcely a dog's chance unless both forwards and backs are strengthened. More strength is wanted in the one plaoe and more speed in the other. In the front rank the improvement is m :et imperative and men: of weight and stamina must be found if the CUP has to Come to Warrington. EvHa the Swinton backs would be comparatively harmless behind a beaten pack, and it is in this department that the committee must enAeavour to secure Warrington the pull when the time comes. The Swinton eight will want some beating, but they will have to be beaten if the scoring powers of the backs are to be checked effectually. These suggestions will need consideration between now and the date of the final.

Warrington's game s'iruggle with tho Blues provided the spectators with plenty of good football, and the match had scarcely a dull moment. Bad fielding lost the home team much ground in the first half,the visitors shining with uncommon refulgence in the running and punting line. Some of the passing was far from being poor ad times and a try ongnt ti have been the outcome once, bat Dicke'son was at fault at the critical moment. In tne second half the Blues soon got the lead by a try, and at three-quarter time they still led by this small margin. In the last quarter, however, the backs simply ran riot and by superb combination coupled with immense speed and dash they raised the score to 11 points. Warrington had no chance of stepping any of the tries, while Cnorley's drop-kick;at the finish was a startler. _

It was quite a treat to see old " Jim" Valentine operating once more in the centre position with 17 years football behind him. He is far from being done yet, and the man who tells me he is fit for nothing but for- ward play will meet with a flat denial, "Jim" played almost as well as ever I saw him play, on Saturday, and I the tryqtageored was worth seeing. There was the Fame old wiline'ss,the same careful attention to the wing man, and nearly the same irresistible dash. He and his brother formed a dangerous pair of centres, and the fact that both scored is significant. Lewis got his usual try by sheer speed, the other wing- man, Wall work, being poor. He made one good run which would have added to the score but for Hallam. 'a resolute tackling,. The Warrington full back again played well and earned high praise from the Swinton crowd. Morgan was the most efficient of the two home halves, Davies being pertara too well watched by Burgess and Bate, who played very fairly. They might I have passed out oftener even against Swinton. Sicking gained little in the second half. Boardman, Pens betton and Taylor were the best of the Warrington forwards. The League table up to date is as follows : For Agst. P. W. L. D. G. T. P. aT. P. Oldham, as well as Swinton, still go on winning, and like the leaders they have a knack of keeping something " up the s'eeve" for emergencies. At Widnes on Saturday they were vigorously handled up to half-time, when the Chemicals were in the proud position of leading by a goal to nil. Their hopes were soon damped in the second moiety, for she Oldham men put all in and scored six tries off the reel. This sneaks well for their fitness to " take in and do for " the Blues at Watersheddings to-day. It should be a great game even should both 4i4s are handicapped by the absence of crack ayers.l wiliiams,Oldham, and Davies. Swinton, are donbtfu starters owing to injuries, which is an unfortunate cir- cumstanoq for all olncerned. Should Swinton Hose they will still have a clear lead of two points and remain the prospective champions.

• Barrow are improving steadily and it will surPrise snme people to learn that they are in a better position than Warrington as regards points, being only one behind and having a match in hand. They have yet to come to Wilderspool, however, and receive a thrashing in return for one administered. On Saturday they sent St. Helena to the right'about by the same scoe that owered Warrington's vaunting ambition at Barrow.
In th, remainlng matches last weelr. Broughton Rangers won creditably at Millom,Stockport were hand- somely thrashed at Lsigh and Runcorn added one more to Rochdale's long list of defeats.

To day's fixture for WarriNgton is with Wigan at Wilderspool. The frost has suddenly disanpeared or a postponent would have been nec•ssary. Such was the case last aewn, and the Wigan match had to be played in mid-week.Warringtnn winning' by a large margin. A week's rest would not do the players much harm. Some oF them have well earned it, and Hallam in particular. H 3 has not missed a match yet.

Warrington " A" accnmoliabed a very smart perform- ance on Saturday in defeating the Swinton men by six points to two points. It was a match entirely of goal- kicking, and to Ratcliffe belonga the credit for all three which stood to Warrington's name at the close. He played a solpndid all-round game in addition,and it will be rank injuatien to kNap him off the 'first team any longer. Langley, Bramhall and Potts, the three juniors who were given a trial, all shaped !promisingly.
